title: Panton, Vermont: background to reading the White letters
text:
Finding census locations on maps
On a mid-October day in 1850, Gaius A. Collum, Assistant Marshall for the U.S. Census, made his way from Panton Village towards Lake Champlain, then headed south along a series of farms bordering the lake. He numbered each residence he visited on that day from 1 to 39 as he recorded their answers to the questions for the 1850 census. Collum followed a path that would be mapped in the mid-1850s by the entrepeneurial cartographer Henry Francis Walling as part of a larger commercial project to produce detailed cadastral maps covering the entire state of Vermont. I have been able to identify locations for about half of the houses where Collum stopped. We can situate these nineteenth-century locations with some confidence thanks to publicly available data sets from the U.S. National Archives1, and from digital archives of nineteenth-century maps.



Gaius Collums’ route on Oct. 15, 1850.


Walling’s printed wall maps of Vermont counties were luxe products. His 1857 map of Addison County (where the census district of Panton is located) spanned more than four feet in each dimension, was printed on four sheets that were then mounted on linen backing, and cost $5 per copy, an exorbitant expenditure at the time. There are two printings of the map with slightly different bordering illustrations, both dated to 1857.2 Both the Library of Congress and the Boston Public Library have digitized copies of the second printing.3 For this post, I worked with a copy of the BPL’s digitization.4



Henry Francis Walling, map of Addison County, Vermont, published 1857.


I georeferenced the map to create a version I could work with using longitude-latitude coordinates.5 Walling’s map includes the surveyed boundary lines of each town in Addison county, most of which are unchanged today. Their clear corners and crossing points provide easy targets to align with modern GIS data from the state of Vermont’s Open Geodata Portal, and are ideally spread across the area of Addison county to yield reasonable results from georeferencing. One inescapabale limit to the accuracy that can be achieved, however, are gaps between the four original printed sheets. Unfortunately the village of Panton falls right on the crossing where all four sheets touch.



Overlay of Wallis’ map on modern dataset showing close alignment of georeferenced nineteenth-century road with modern Route 22A.


Nevertheless, the resulting alignment is very usable. In the illustration above, for example, we can see how closely a modern map of Vermont Route 22A aligns with the same road in the georeferenced version of Wallis’ map. We can also see the detailed plotting with labels of every major house and structure Wallis observed. It was appealing to potential buyers to see their own house on the map – and a gold mine for historians more than a century and a half later. With the georeferenced map in place, I followed Collum’s census listings, and matched names in the census record with labels on Walling’s map.

title: Panton, Vermont: background to reading the White letters
text:
Reading the White letters
We can now trace Gaius Collum’s route on October 15, 1850, house by house. Here, points are labelled with the number Collum assigned to each house, and the name of the head of household in his census record.




From houses 24 (David Adams) to 31 (Horatio N. White), census taker Collum traveled south alongside the east shore of Lake Champlain.



The property at house 31 must have been pleasant: Collum recorded its value as $7,000, a figure exceeded by only 10 of the 56 properties listed with recorded values in the 1850 census for Panton. Collum identified the farmer who lived there as 47-year-old Horatio N. White. This corresponds perfectly with the location of two adjacent buildings that Walling labels “H.N. White Res” and “H.N. White.”
This is also the same Horatio Nelson White who kept a series of family letters that were passed along by five generations of his descendants until they were donated to the American Antiquarian Society (AAS) in 2024.6 In a town with a total population of 559 in the 1850 census, Walling’s “H.N. White” identifies him unambiguously, and “H.N. White, Panton, Vermont,” was in fact the normal address his family used in writing to him, as illustrated in this detail of a letter dated to March of 1857, at exactly the time Walling was surveying and publishing his map of Addison county.



Detail of this full image: address on the cover of a letter from Henry George White, Buffalo, New York, to his brother, Horatio Nelson White in Panton, Vermont.


Connecting information in documentary sources like census records with geographic information can illuminate many aspects of the White letters. For a very simple first example, I will mention the marriage of Horatio Nelson’s son, William E. White, to Ellen Grandey.7 The Vermont state archives records their marriage on November 19, 1859, and helpfully gives us the names of the bride’s parents, Truman and Polly Grandey.
The US Census of 1850 was the first to list individuals by name (rather than just counts of individuals in various categories), so we can follow changes in the makeup of households from decade to decade. In 1850, 14-year-old William White was living with his parents and five siblings. One Truman Grandy and his wife Polly have a daughter Ellen, then age 8. Ten years later, we find William and Ellen together, and a check in the final column illustrated here indicates “Married within the year”.



1860 census entries for William E. and Ellen White checking their status as newlyweds.


Like the Whites, the Grandys also lived in Panton: Horatio Nelson and his family were house 31 on Collum’s itinerary, the Grandys were house 44. Only when we find them both on H.F. Walling’s map is it obvious that Collum’s route from house 31 to house 44 twisted and turned through a cluster of residences at a small crossroads. Despite the large separation in numbering from 31 to 44, the Grandys and Whites were in fact separated only by the distance of a couple of farms. We’ll never know exactly how William and Ellen met, but we’re now free to imagine all the possibilities of two neighboring farming families in a small town in nineteenth-century Vermont.



Relative location of White and Grandy families, houses 31 and 44 in the 1850 census for Panton.

title: A cheatsheet for reading the White family letters
text:
I’m about halfway through initial transcriptions of the White letters, and so far have encountered references to twenty-four different members of the White family spread across three generations. Nicknames, preference for middle or first names and accompanying free variation in the order of names, and generosity in honoring other family members with repeated names can make these difficult to keep straight. James Herbert White appears in census records as “James H.” but can be “Bertie” in letters. I have not seen any instance of Candace Myra White’s full name: she can be Candace M., Myra C., or just Myra (or Mira). Hirams, Georges and Henrys all proliferate across many generations of the White family.
I’ve put together this summary chart to help me or anyone else who dips into the letters. It is (intentionally) not a complete family tree: it shows the family relations only of names I have found in the letters, all of which fall between 1842 and 1860. Other family members (whether previously deceased, not yet born or married into the family, or simply not mentioned in the letters) do not appear here.

title: A cheatsheet for reading the White family letters
text:
Linked information
The links on each name lead to automatically generated pages. These pages list source material that I have both transcribed (including material outside the White letters) and indexed to the individual, and summarize conclusions about the chronology and family relations of the individual that can be derived from the transcribed sources. Transcribing and indexing each source is slow work, but it means that automated summaries for each person cannot present conclusions without some underlying documentary evidence. As I continue to work on documenting the individuals listed here, I hope that the automated aggregation of source material will be increasingly useful to readers of the White letters or others interested in topics of family or local history involving members of the White family.

title: A cheatsheet for reading the White family letters
text:
Follow the project’s progress
I’m using the tag White letters as I post new content about the White family letters project. You can either look for the tag on the list of posts, or follow a direct link to White letters.
If you’re interested in how I manage the information to generate this web site, I’ll use the tag DIY history for posts on that topic.

text:
Transcription
“HIGH” WHITE DEAD.

He Passed Away Yesterday in the 77th Year of His Age.
Hiram White died yesterday morning in the 77th year of his age. He was one of the city’s oldest residents. In his early life he was very active. When the gold craze spread over the country he was one of the many who went to California. Gold not being as plentiful as he anticipated he came back and settled down contented. He captained a canal boat for years, run a grocery store for a time and in his later years lived upon a farm. He was successful in all these pursuits and accumulated considerable property.
In his prime Mr. White was an active member of the Boxer Engine company and was always more or less mixed up in politics, being a “dyed-in-the-wood” democrat. He served as constable and collector of taxes. This gave him a wide acquaintance and be was familiarly known by all as “High” White. He was, also, a member of the Howard Guards. Though eccentric in his ways, he bad many admirable traits.
A wife and son survive him.

H. G. WHITE DIES VERY SUDDENLY.

WAS ONE OF BUFFALO’S OLDEST CITIZENS - BORN AT BURLINGTON, VT., IN 1814
HERE FOR YEARS.

Henry George White, one of Buffalo’s oldest residents.and one of the city’s most esteemed citizens, died at his home, No, 32 Irving Place, at 6 o’clock this morning. Death, although resulting from old age, was unexpected. Last night Mr. White retired as well as he has ever been during the past two years, and this morning he was discovered dying by one of the members of the family. A physician was summoned but dying expired as the physician crossed the threshold.
Mr. White was borning in Burlington, Vt.. June 8, 1814..

Louise N. Gattis
Services for Mrs. Louise Neel Gattis, 83, Murfreesboro, who died at home Thursday, are set for 3 p.m. Sunday at First United Methodist Church.
Her parents were the late Robert and Willie Blanton Neel and her husband was the late Claud Gattis.
She is survied by two daughters, Judy Gattis Smith of Richmond, Va., Gloria Gattis ANdrews of Murfreesboro; five grandchildren; and seven great-grandchildren.
She was a member of the Murfreesboro Women’s Club, United Daughters of the Conferederacy, Delta Kappa Gamma honorary educational society, Retired Teachers Association and the First United Methodist Church. She taught at McFadden School for 32 years.
Memorial contributions may be made to her church, Linebaugh Library, or to Hospice of Murfreesboro.
Visitation will be held from 2-4 p.m. Saturday at Jennings & Ayers Funeral Home.
Daily News Journal, Nov. 24, 1995.

Funeral Services Conducted for I.N. Gattis, 73
Funeral services were held from the residence on Church St. today at 10:30 o’clock for I.N. Gattis, 73, who died at Sarasota, Fla., at 6 p.m. Saturday following a heart attack.
He was a native of Bedford county but had made his home here for the past 25 years. Until his health failed, he was prominently identified with music houses throughout the south. He was a member of the First Methodist church.
He is survived by his wife, Mrs. Cassie Green Gattis; two daughters, Mrs. Will Gilmore of Murfreesboro and Mrs. E. W. Hill of Chattanooga, a son, Claude Gattis of Murfreesboro, and five grandchildren.
The funeral services were conducted by the Rev. Neal Frazier and the Rev. B.B. Pennington. Burial was at Evergreen cemetery under the direction of Woodfin-Moore.
Pallbearers were A.H. Smith, Tom McCord, T.S. McFerrin, William Earthman Will Co[illegible], E.C. Holloway, Sr. and Fr[illegieble]ry.

NORMAN, Bee Neel, 87, passed away on December 11, 1998. Retired from Technicolor Corp. Bee was a resident of North Hollywood for nearly forty years. She was the beloved wife of Geoffrey Norman, who passed away in 1985. Bee is survived by her sons, Richard Ellard, of Valencia and Robert Howard, of Fairhaven, Washington; her step-daughter, Jozanne Dyer, of South Hampton, England; and her step-niece, Caroline Reisch of Wolfsburg, Germany. Known for her independence, wit and beauty, Bee will be greatly missed by her family, friends and neighbors.
A private gathering in her memory is pending.
In lieu of flowers, donations may be made in Bee’s memory to a charity of one’s choice.

Visitation with the family be help from 7 to 9 tonight at Jennings & Ayers Chapel.

Miss Judy Gattis Completes Wedding Plans; Pre-Nuptial Parties to be Given
Miss Judy Gattis has chosen April 9 as the date for her marriage to David Hammond Smith of Cambria, Virginia.
Stanford Memorial Chapel, Oak Hill First Presbyterian church, Nashville, will be the scene of the morning ceremony with Dr. Walter R. Courtenay officiating at eleven o’clock.
Preceding the reading of the vows a program of nuptial music will be presented by Roberta Womac, vocalist, and Cyrus Daniel, organist.
Mr. Gattis will give his daughter in marriage and Miss Gloria Gattis of Milligan college, Tennessee, sister of the bride, will be the only attendant.
Ensign Charles Richard Smith will serve as his brother’s best man and ushers will be George M. Bell and R. Kolmar Altizer of Cambria, Virginia.
Following the wedding, Mr. and Mrs. Gattis will entertain at a breakfast at Oak Hill. Assisting with the affair will be Miss Jan Dourhit, Miss Betty Ray Clark, Miss Frances Smith, Miss Glover Dale Tarver and Misses Sara Jo and Nancy Wallen.

Obituary
Mrs. James A. Merrill died very suddenly Saturday afternoon at her home in Burlington, after a week’s illness with angina pectoris aged 43. She had not been considered critically ill and only an hour before her death she had assured her husband that she felt much better.
Mrs. Merrill was born in Panton, the daughter of William E. and Ellen M. White. In 1892 she was married to Mr. Merrill and after living in Panton for three years, they went to Burlington, in which city they have since resided. Besides her husband, Mrs. Merrill is survived by three daugthers, Elsie, Marguerite and Helen; two brothers, Walter White of Panton and George White of Worcester, Mass.; and two sisters, Mrs. Frank Randall of Pasadena, Cal., and Mrs. George W. Hatch of Burlington. The funeral services were held Tuesday morning at the house and were private. Interment was made in Lakeview cemetery, Burlington.

Transcription

First page
Will of Sallie T. Williams, deceased.

I, Sallie T. Williams, being of sound mind and disposing memory, do make and publish this my last will and testament, herby rvoking any other will made by me.
Item First. I direct the payment of any just debt that I may be owing at the time of my death, together with my funeral and burial expenses, out of the first money that may come into the hands of my executors herinafter named. Item Two. If the graves of my husband, David Williams, Sr., and my son, David Williams, Jr., and my daughter Lavenia Williams, have not been propertly marked at the time of my death, my executor is directed to do so, using such amount therefor as he may deem right and proper in the exercise of his discretion. Item Three. All the balance of my estate of every kind and description I give and bequeath in equal amounts as follows:- one share to my daughter, Elivra Ann Green, wife of J.G. Green; one share to Normer Barber Williams and her sister, Nellie Barber Turrentine, wife of Sam Turrentine; one share to Minnie Williams and Mary Williams, my grandchildren, the children of my deceased son David Williams, Jr. Item Fourth. I nominate and appoint J.G. Green and wilfe Elivira Ann Green executors of this my last will and testament.
Sallie T. Williams
We the undersigned have attached our names hereto as attesting witnesses in the presence and at the request of the testatrix, who sigbned the above in our presence as her last will and testament and we have signed as attesting witnesses in the presence of each other, This the – day of – 1902.
Saml. L. Knox Joe Landers
I, J.G. Green, make oath that the above is a true and perfect copy of the last will and testament of Sallie T. Williams, deceased, as nearly aas I can give the same from memory, the original of which was destroyed by L.B. Williams in my presence on Oct. 14, 1910.
J.G. Green
sworn to and subscribed before me, this October 26th, 1910. E.W. Bearden, [??]



Second page
Certificate of Clerk and master State of Tennessee County of Bedford,
I, E.W. Bearden, clerk and master of the Chancery Court at Shelbyville, do certify that the within and foregoing is a full, true and perfect copy of the last will and testament of Sallie T. Williams, deceased, as set up and established by decree of Chancery Court rendered on Nov. 8th, 1910, and entered in Minute book “Q” (?) pages 481 et seq. in said Court the cause therein of “J.G. Green et als. vs. L.B. Williams”. Said will was, by said decree, ordered to be certified to the County Court of Bedford County, Tenn., there to be proceeded on and under as the last will and testament of said Sallie T. Williams, deceased. Witness my hand and seal of office, in Shelbyville, Tenn., this Nov 10th., 1910, E.W. Bearden, Clerk & Master State of Tennessee. Bedford County.
I, P.C. Steele, County Court Clerk of Bedford County, do herby certify tht the foregoing is a full, true and perfect copy of the last will and testament of Sallie T. Williams, deceased, as certifeid to this court by E.W. Bearden, Clerk & Master of the Chancery Court at Shelbyville, Tenn, and admitted to probate in the County Court of Bedford County on the 14th day of November, 1910. and order to be recroded as the last will and testament of Sallie T. Williams, as shows by certified copy now on file in my office. Witness my hand at office this the 14th day Nov. 1910, P.C. Steele, Clear, By Jo.D.Steele D.C.

first, I give and bequet to my son Kindred
the horse that he now Claimes with Sadle and bridle and one Feather Bed and Furniture
I Give and Bequeath to my Son Eleazer
one Cott that he now clames, Sadle and Bridle
one Bed and Furniture
Thirdly I give unto my Beloved Wife Martha
All the rest of my personal property Except such things as the Family Can Best Share Sufficient to pay all my Just Debts Also all my Lands During the Natural life or widowhood To raise the Children uppon and that She when my Daughter Sarah Comes of age to receive in good property or Money to the Amount of Eighty Dollars & to my Daughter Mirium the Same to wit Eighty Dollars
and to my Son Burrel Eighty Dollars in some good property or Money
and to my Daughter Ceily Ann - Eighty Dollars

text:
Transcription
James Rices Will
In the name of God. Amen.
I James Rice of Barre in the County of Worcester Yeoman, being weak in Body , but of sound and disposing mind and memory, blessed be God for the same, do make this my last Will and Testament this fifteenth day of July, in the year of our Lord, One thousand, eight hundred and thirty two, as follows viz.
I recommend my Soul to God who gave it.
Firstly. I will and direct that my Executor hereafter named, provide and support my beloved Wife during her natural life, comfortably and furnish her with all things necessary for her in sickness and health, and at her decease, a decent burial. my said Wife is to have the use and improvement of my House hold Furniture during her life, and after her decease to be equally divided among my Heirs.
Secondly. I give and bequeath unto my son Samuel Rice, his heirs and assigns forever, all my Homestead Farm situate and lying in Barre & Petersham which is now owned and lies in common between us. Also the Brinknal lot, so called, the Mann lot, so called, and Mill lot, so called. Said last mentioned lot lies in Petersham, and also the Hammond lot, so called. Also I give unto the said Samuel Rice, all my Stock and Farming Tools, to be at his own disposal forever. also my Pew in Barre Meeting House.
Thirdly. I give and bequeath unto my Grandchildren hereafter named, their heirs, etc., to wit, Clarissa Miller wife, Schuyler Miller, the sum of seventy-five Dollars, to be paid by my Executor, in one year after my decease. Also I give unto my other Grandchildren Lucretia Partridge and Lucy Rice to each of them I give the sum of seventy five dollars to be paid them by my Executor hereafter named, in one year after my decease.
Fourthly. To the Heirs of Freeman Rice, I give nothing. I give to Alfred Cladwell, son of Susan Wilder, two hundred dollars, to be paid him by my Executor in one year after my death.
Fifthly and lastly. As to the residue of all my property after paying out my just debts and funeral expenses which property is not before named, I give & bequeath the same to my Sons viz. Sparahawk Rice, Ralph Rice and Nahah Rice, their heirs etc to be equally divided between them.
I direct my Executor to sell all my Real Estate not before disposed of, as soon as convenient after my decease, and apply the proceeds as before divided, as also the remainder of my personal property.
I hereby appoint my Son Samuel, sole Executor of this my last Will and Testament, hereby revoking all other and former Wills, by me made.
In Witness whereof, I hve hereunto set my hand and seal, the day and year above written.
James x Rice his mark
Signed, sealed, published and declared by the said James Rice to be his last WIll and Testament in presence of us, who are called as Witnesses to the same by said Rice, and have signed our names to the same in his presence.
Nath. Houghton
Anson Bates
Charles Rice
Worcester. To all people to whom these presents shall come, Nath. Paine Esq. Judge of Probate of Wills, etc in the County of Worcester within the Commonwealt of Massachusetts, sendeth Greeting

title: neelsmith
text:
Transcription
Daniel C. Henderson
County of Herkimer Surrogate Court
In the Matter of proving the last will and testament of Daniel C. Henderson Deceased
Herkimer County fo Elias B. Pullman of the Town of Norway in the County of Herkimer being first Sworn in Open Court on their Oaths do depose and say that the said deceased did in the presence of these deponents subscribe his name at the end of the instrument which is now shown to these deponents and which purportz to be the last will and testament of the said Deceased and which bears date on the 17th day of January A.D. 1860 that the said Deceased did at the time of subscribing his name to said instrument as aforesid declair the same to be his last will and testament that these deponents did thereupon subscribe their names at the end of said instrument as attesting Witness to the execution thereof at the request of the said Deceased and in his presence and in the presence of each Other That the said Deceased at the time of subscribing his name to said instrument as aforesaid has upwards of twenty one years of age that he appears to be of sound mind and memory and was not under restraint to the knowledge or belief of these deponents
Sworn examened and subscribed this 1st day of October 1860 before me Ezra Graves Surrogate
Sarah Pullman
Elias B. Pullman
I Daniel C Henderson of the Town of Norway County of Herkimer State of New York being deeply impressed by the ?im…lantly? of human Life doest Constitute this my last will and testament in the Manner following 1st To my beloved Wife Margaret besides her right of Dower it is my will that she retain in her full possession of the house and lot togethger with the household furniture during her natural lifetime or so long as she remains my Widow
2nd To my son Dryden Henderson I devise and bequeath my House and lot called the Mason House and the store and lot called the Beadley Store to him my son Dryden of his full share of my estate after the deceast of my beloved wife Margaret
Let it be understood that I have lately bought a lot of some twenty Acres 20% called the Pullman lot which is not all paid for now what is not paid at my deceast my three sons Dryden Nathaniel and John D. Henderson must equally pay or caused to be paid after the Bond I gave for the payment for the lot called the Pullman lot my three sons Dryden Nathaniel and John D Henderson must pay each one Hundred Dollars to my youngest Daughter Sarah Bragg to whom I devise and give the lot called the Pullman lot as her full share of my Estate excepting what is hereafter mentioned
To my four Grand Children heirs of my son Hugh deseast I bequeath to Margaret Henderson fifty Dollars to Daniel C James E & John D Henderson my Grand Children one hundred Dollars each to be paid in three and four years after my decest by my executors after the deceast of my beloved wife the house hold furniture is to be Equally divided between my three Daughters Mary Ann Tillinghast Juliette M Johnson and Sarah Bragg after all Claims and bequeaths debts are paid the rest of my property consisting of Mortgatges Bonds or Notes accounts or any note heretofore mentioned of whatever name or nature that except heretofore or hereafter is to be equally divided between my Children mentioned hereafter viz Nathaniel S Henderson John D Henderson Mary Ann Tillinghast Juliette M John son My Libra? such as it is to divided Equally between my three sons heretofore named If theire are Carrages of any kind Waggon be eather at my deceast my son Dryden Henderson must have my Old Natch I give to my Grand son Horace Bragg
Lastly I hereby appoint my son Dryden and Nathaniel S Henderson my executors of this my last will and testament hereby revoking all former will by me made
Daniel C Henderson
In witness whereof I have hereunto set my hand and affixed my seal this seventeenth day of January one Thousand Eight Hundred and Sixty Signed Sealed published and delivered be the above named Daniel C Henderson to be his last will and testament in presence of us who have hereunto subscribed Our Names as Witnesses in presence of the testator and at his request
Elias B Pullman Norway Sarah Pullman Norway
County of Herkimer
Surrogate Office for
Be it remembered that on the day of the date hereof the last will and testament of Daniel C Henderson late of Norway in the County of Herkimer Deceased bearing date 17th day of January One Thousand Eight Hundred and Sixty
(certification of copy continues on following page)

title: neelsmith
text:
Synopsis
Ebenezer in Burlington writes to Horatio Nelson in Panton.
Ebenezer provides a full acount of everyone’s health, as well as treating his own own ailments with homeopathic pills that George sent to him.

title: neelsmith
text:
Transcription
Burlington March 2nd 1851
My Son
I did not expect to write you until I had seen you I expected you were here before this. Francis writes that you are nomore likely to be ready than you ware months ago. I am prety smart for me Adaline sliped down on the platform East door last monday week and sprained her wrist very bad we thought it was broke at first but the Doctor sais it is not but it will take longer to heal than if the bone had ben broken I reced a letter from Geo. yesterday 8 oclock A.M. with two little Bottls of Homapathy pills about the Size of Mustard seid directions to take 5 of one kind at night 5 of the other in the morning with a printed Directions what I might eat & Drink and what is prohibited, amongst the greatest comforts of life was that of Tobaco, so I laid my pipe on the stove and went to preparing and last night I took 5 and 5 this morning. I feel no better my head flies round like a top oh! my Tobacco I miss it more than all the rest but I will try to get along but have not Faith the bigness of one of the pils. George’s Charles has ben verry Sick, but had got about well (?) sais he has writen to you twice but has had no answer I think that , Friend wont be likely to fall in Love with work immedately on his return from School I think he has improved his ways are easey and quite agreeable I think he would like to go through Colledge Give my love to all hope you are all well I shant watch at the South window any more for you for when you come we shall know it I had most forgotten Hiram we hear from him evry Mail by some one who writes, and Cynthia has one letter from him Since Friend was here and expect one next tuesday or wedensday he said he should write Father a Thundering letter, I expect it will come on the Telegraph. So if you are up here you will have a chance to read it if you please I have a miserable pen and I believe if I had a larger Chaw of Tobacco my hand would be more stidy you Father E. White

title: neelsmith
text:
Buffalo 7th Nov 1856
Sunday Evening Windy & Rain
Brother Nelson & Family
Your last letter came duly to hand & found us as it left you all in a very comfortable state of health
We of course were glad to hear from you once more, indeed as always are glad to hear from you one & all – you write that all are at home – please say to William that I should be pleased to have him write to me whenever he feels like it, as also Frances they both owe me one I think, and if my namesake or Candace will write I will answer

title: neelsmith
text:
Ebenezer in Burlington writes to Horatio Nelson in Panton.
Ebenezer replies to a request from Horatio Nelson for information about a payment of $730.00 to “Englesby”. This is Ebenezer Torrey Englesby, who is known from the Vermont Historical Archives. Ebenezer and his sons Horatio Nelson and Artemas all seem to be involved in this transaction in some way.
Ebenezer reports on Horatio Nelson’s mother and sister, Adaline, both of whom are living with him in Burlington at this time, and shares news from Horatio Nelson’s siblings Artemas, whom Ebenezer has seen, and George , via letter from Buffalo. Ebenezer closes by inquiring after his grandson, Fran (Frances E. White).

title: neelsmith
text:
Transcription
Burlington July 17 1842 About 3 oclock pm.
Dear Son
I reced a letter from you bearing date 6th of may which I expect mant to be the 6th of June. it was Mailed at Westport June 9th informing me of your hard headacke &c wishing me to get the amount of what you paid to Englesby which I have done for I found the Note you gave him with the rest of His old papers which I preserved so there can be no mistake on that subject the amount of Principle & Intrest amounted at the time I lost it to $731.00 I have seen Artemas, and he says he will do as you do about it, so I see no dificulty in the way only for us to ?? the money which I cannot tell how Soon as we can not collect our Boot debet just yet. you wished me to say to your mother & Adaline Somthing about ?Fetching? &c they both nead the ?Lettin? &c and that is sufficient I should be glad to hear from you all, the pneumoliny sickness has abated I reced a Letter from Artemas informing us that his Wife has taken a cold in the Late Rain Storm an has got a relapse & that her simptoms are unharming. She was over here about thee weeks since and staid a wee (sic) or there abouts and went home quite smart, all but well and we had reason to hope she would fully recover her health if carefull but it apeard to be otherwise. he also writes that all of his children are quite unwell & that himself is far from being well I think he has a great deal of sickness in his family, but it is all right for God doth it & he can do no wrong you will remember him at the Throne of God I have recd three letters from George since I sawy you Both by private convayance they ware all well & it was healthy in that place but he is not doing as much Buisness as usual on account of the Scarcity of cash and that his partner (Smith) is about to desolve and go to St Luis where he thinks he can do better. it will a disapointment to George, but so it goes. he says you have not written to him yet, and he further says that your Smileing about weaning the boy is lost for there is no such thing as you suspect Adaline has ben Sick but we are now all well thanks be to God Rember our best Love to all your family I hope you are all well I have a fine Garden & so has every body that has kept clean of weeds ?? all Look Finely
your Father
P.S. Remember us to Fran old Sport I hope he behave well & that you will treat him well I felt Sory to hear this poor old Fellow Cry when he left us EW
I have written to Artemas V. George to day & shall attend the Service I attende the forenoon

title: neelsmith
text:
Notes
“Mary White”, a visitor and presumably relative, is probably Mary Ella White. She would be 16 at the time, and her father Artemas is probably still in California.
Sept 19 1850 census in Keeseville finds Artemas at home…
Who is “Hopkins”? ## Synopsis
Hiram in Burlington writes to Horatio Nelson and his family in Panton.
Hiram has caught the “gold fevour” and nothing can dissuade him from going to California. He is following in the tracks of his brother, Artemas, who went west in five monts earlier (in November, 1849: see 1849-11-18-EW-to-HNW). Like Artemas, Hiram would return home before the end of 1850: the census that year shows him with his family in Burlington on August 20.

title: neelsmith
text:
Transcription
Burlington April 7th 1850
Dear Brother Sister and All As you wrote me a Considerable long letter some time since I fell it my duty to return the same you wrote me that if you thought it would have any weight in stopping me from going to California you would write a sermon I am verry glad you did not for it would not have the least impression on me go I must. Although I think my silf if I could of contented my self at home and be satisfied with my business It would of ben better for me But I have got the fevour and have had it eve sence the first gold was found and since that time I have ben determined to go my mind has not ben on my business nor nothing has ben aright with it The reason is I could not attend to it as had oughto
By this you can see my reasens for going. But enuff of this I mooved last saturday and have got all things streightend out I shall start next wednesday morning in the southern cars if nothing happens more then I now see There will probably be some from vergenz along at the same time but strangers to me most of them but they are agoing in the same ship and probably I shall git acquainted with them. I have moooved my Family to Fathers they are very comfortably situated considering. You may expect a long visit from Cynthia this summer is she is well enufff to go she has got to visit for the purpus of saving her house I tell her. Mary White is here and has ben for about a fornit. I hope she will leave soon for the good of —
If I live to get to California I shall write you a letter I you will do me the same in return and then I will tell you wether that Hopkins has ben Cropped or not Tell Friend not to think of going nor lit such a thought remain in his head for as long as his mind is on the Yellow stuff he nor no one if fit for any other business In the first place he is to young if he had the means given to him and another thing he has not seen enuff of the deceit of this world I have had a chance of seeing considerible more than he has and call my self a regular green one I am but an infant among them tell him for me to hold on untill I write home for if I cannot git some he had not better try. Francis is well and is looking very anxious for a letter she has ben sore lonesome here but I think she will not be so much. My Heifer I thought you would not want for the day I got your letter she was a playing a trick that led me to think she was not acoming in any I expected so I sold her to the Butchers My cow I lent to Father his he sold My Turkeys I sold My Dog was the worst of the lot when I led him away I thought If I had neve thought of going I should of ben glad But all this is nothing whin I come to bid my Family and other Friends I hold dear good buy prehaps foreve that is the trying all for gold the gold I want but I wish it was not so far But it to late now to think of these things go I must It would be the ruin of me to stay heer now and it cannot be no more if I go
Give my love to all
Good By Hiram

title: neelsmith
text:
Transcription
Buffalo 3d Sept 1851
My Dear Brother & family,
You undoubtedly think it quite strange that I do not write to You in answer to Yours of the 5th Aug but when You know the reasons You will be satisfied
We went up into Ohio to see a Sister of My Wife whom she had not seen for about fifteen years I went with her as no one did know about the point to leave the Railroad as she lived in a small country village some 8 miles from the line of travel I went with her & after staying I came back on my return intending to stay one day with her brother but found him sick & stayed 10 days & left My wife there & today I reced a telegraph stating he had died at noon Ann is still there & will no doubt providence permitting be with me on Saturday So you see our visit of pleasure ended in sorrow not that we went for we were glad to minister to his wants but we did not expect to see him quite so low, as he had left our house quite comfortable about 3 weeks before, his disease was quick consumption he was the best of Brothers
We were glad to recieve so long a letter from you & that you were all so well for it is a source of real pleasure receve a letter from those we care for & that care for us in return
I would not wish to spin out this letter to an unusual length nor would I wish to hide from you our pleasure that you were coming to see us & hope your haying has gone off to suit you & that you will come do not let us be disapointed this time for it is too bad to be so, I have always said if you only had your minds made up you were half here & it is so. for the facilities are such you can come here in one & half days if you choose to do so, I will not enumerate to you all the inducements for you to come but one of them is that I hope you will meet with a welcome from each of us & you will be repaying some of your many debts due us which will be a source of pleasure no doubt
I was glad to hear from Hiram although he does never find time to write to me even one little scrap notwithstanding I have written as many as four to him & paid the postage on some of them too but no doubt he depends much upon my forbearance & good nature to overlook his deficiencies – his wife wrote to me a letter that I answered on Sunday I am sorry that she is not as well as last Year but hope she may get better soon I have invited her often to come & see us & bring Henry with her
You say that you have all visited Burlington since I was at your house I regret that I have not but I somehow thought I would like to see you or some of you out here & so defered my visit waiting for you
I say I regret that I had never been there since the melancholy time I was there to bury my own dear Mother the best of earthly friends I know it would not be now as formerly & should not expect it, but I do not forget it would afford a pleasure to my father to have me come & see him again & I have promised him to come again soon I would like to come & go & see you all if I had time & means to do so for I have the desire
I shall write to Father & Artemas soon I am glad that Friend gets along so well with his studies & hope he will aim high in all his aspirations after knowledge ever bearing in mind to do all things well I would be glad to have him & Frances or any of you come over & see us
Our children are all quite well & write in sending love to all their Cousins Uncles & Aunts in your vicinity
Excuse this as it is the 3rd this evening
Your Brother
H.G. White

title: neelsmith
text:
Transcription
Burlington Oct. 30 1851
My Son Nelson There was a time when I and you used to corrispond by letter, but that time appears to be past and gone by whose falt whether my own or yours I am not able to tell when I wrote to you or you to me. I should like on my part to renew that corispondenceces tharefore I now begin I have nothing in particular to write but will write to let you know I think of you & care for you we are as well as usual. hoping these few lines will find you enjoying the same blessings it seems to me you have not paid us a visit for a very long time I don’t remember, but one thing I remember that is that little rogue of a Candace has not ben to see us for a long, long tim, we all want to see her very much she must not let those fals reports deter her coming for I think we all love her I should love her if it ware only for her name which will ever be Dear to me. I was disappinted to learn that -that- you had given up going to Buffalo I ware sory for it, but undoubtedly you know your own buisness better than I do, but it does appear to me that you never will have a better time if as good. I rec’d a letter from George a few day since they ware still hoping and expecting you wold yet come, but they will hope in vain I do not think now that you ever will see Buffalo, you have talked so much about it without caning the talk into affect. I hope Friend will go and see his uncle George when he arrive at the age of 21 and Frances when she becomes 18 and so on if they all live. George tells of coming out here in the winter he can as well come in the winter as any time we had or Cynthia had a letter from Hiram the maile before the last he does not say how he is doing only he is drawing dirt with his Mule and Cart to the River to wash and that he is as Fat as a Bear & Black as an Indian but does not tell of ever coming hom. I suppose Cynthia has told all to Francies as I understan they are in corispondane with each other and now I have writen to you I shall expect you will return the complement it is only just three cents as Jack Pomroy said when some of you boys found a bundle of his papers and ran all over Toronto to give them to him one cold night he said here is just six cents I do not send my compliments to you and Family but I real love to you all
you Father Ebenr White
H.N. White Esq.
Henry says you come within two votes of going to the legislator
Brother Nelson
I wish to know if you could put me down 30 or 40 pounds of Butter if so you may get a tub and put it in and if it would come safe in the cars put it aboard if none of you are coming up, I should be glad if I could get a fat hog but do not know how it would be about getting it here you will please inform me how it is,
Yours Adaline
N.B. everything you send will be so much my gane.
E.W.

Buffalo 13th Dec 1857
My Eldest Brother
Your ery kind letter came duly to hand, for which I thank you for it has opened again a vein of affectionate sympathy that had been too long closed at one end at least, – I say that I realy feel thankful for it, for one of the comforts of my life is to think that I love am beloved in turn by my kindred & however I may at times manifest my love God knows that I realy love all & desire their true happiness –

Henry George White in Buffalo writes to Horatio Nelson White in Panton.
Henry George adduces numerous arguments to persuade Horatio Nelson to come to Buffalo for a visit. These include details of local travel that is now so much easier in “the Cars” than with the earlier stage or canal journey (a mere 36 hours from Panton to Buffalo!), the many sights such as the wire suspension bridge at Niagara Falls, and along with the other conveniences in Buffalo “all Sorts of Meeting Houses.”

title: neelsmith
text:
Transcription
Buffalo 26th Oct. 1851
Dear Brother & Sister
I recd a letter from Father last night & by it I learned that you had about made up your minds not to “come and see” us, I need not to tell you how much we were disapointed, for you will probably have expected that after so many years of promise & waiting to thus be deprived of an expected pleasure —
I do not know what is the cause of your altering your minds, nor do I mean to question you concerning it, for you are both of you competent to manage your own affairs to suit yourselves
We would be glad if still you would come this fall for although it now snows a trifle it will in all human probability clear off & and then quite a “spell of good & pleasant weather will follow” during which you would have a good time to come & pay us a visit – it is not now so great an undertaking as it was formerly for you know now a ride in the Cars is quite a comfortable thing to what it was upon the canal or stage & time is anhialated for if you leave Your own House in the afternoon of Wednesday Thursday night will undoubtedly find you at our House
So you see it is only 36 hours ride at the most, quite a short affair & we hope you will try it – now I do not thus write to tell you what you do not know already only to stir you up to action by holding up to your view the feasebility of the thing & probably you will never have a better time to come than now, for you now have a man to leave with the affairs of the farm outdoors & a woman to look well after the things in the House & they are both well known to you & if you choose to take one of the small ones it will not cost you anything for I never paid anything for Anna Elisa when we went to Ohio & I saw Samuel Dresen on his way home from Burlington to the West & he had a wife & two children of the ages of 4 & 11 Years & he said he did not pay anything for them all the way out & back & took a first passage at that, so You see if You do not like to leave all take one or more along as it will not cost you anything & we would like to have the small ones pleased
Brother & Sister I would urge You by every consideration to Come & I promise to make all except the weather pleasant & will hope & pray for that even, so that there will be nothing in the way.
Our 3 children write with us in urging you to come out here for you know all children like to see their uncles & Aunts & Cousins So come along
The weather this fall has been quite changeable & today we have had our first snow storm but I hope it will not be a beginning of winter for we usualy do not have it so soon here so dont be frightened from coming by fears of winter
We are all quite well at present & trust a continuation of the Same Sort as we are cold water users & Homeopathists & with them both trust to preserve a tolerable share of health &c so dont expect to find us sick for we seldom are & if you are when you get here, there is all Sorts of good doctors & you will be taken care of I assure you
I have plenty of every thing except Cash & can get enough for all practical purposes of that & I have no doubt you will be made comfortable while you are here
There are all Sorts of Meeting Houses here & you can be suplied with any Sort of worship & there is a Methodist place of worship within Seventy rods of our House & a smart(?) man to preach to all who choose to come & hear, but the place we attend is somewhat futher off So you see you can be suited in all things
Niagara Falls is within one hours ride of our house & there is a wire suspension bridge there which is well worth a ride from your home to here to see, independent of the falls which are some so they say, but I need not enumerate the many things to be seen on your way & while here & about here & on you way out here nor the good you will both recieve Moraly Physicaly & Intelectualy I mean the benefit to Body & Soul & every thing else to be benefited by a trip of a day & a half across one of the states “as is a state”
I wrote to Father last Sunday & recd one from him Yesterday informing me of another nephew at Keeseville if I were they I would quit & “cry enough”

title: neelsmith
text:
Transcription
Tell H N White that I believe the said Doctor allin to be a great Humbug & Liar & that instead of having the Doctors under his controll they discountenanced him altogether & that his associates were of not the most respectable character & that instead of his being Rich as he represented himself to be his was verry poor & that I think he will not molest Jewett for the more Some things are stired the worse it is When he came back here he had Several hundred dollars with him no doubt obtained from Some of his dupes poor Simple fools way down in Vermont You know that Jo Smith had his believers & that people that are honest are prone to believe all bold pretenders honest likewise especialy if they do not look cooly at the things as they pass, he had (I mean Allein) but one or two who believed anything he said in this city & now has gone off from here & left his babe with strangers promising to return soon & whether he will do so or not remains to be seen Yet at any rate many do not believe he will call for the child he boarded while here with one Lindsay a Swinestealer & the man Barker So far as I know is an Honest respectable man & has been helped by him as he believes but whether or no such is the case I am led to doubt for perhaps nature done the most for him after all the others that he helped as he aren any men that have been ailing for some time & no doubt some what whimsical & their mind only to be doctored by one who could boldly affirm he could do some great thing & they would fancy themselves well again
I do not wish to get into any fuss with the aforesaid doctor nor do I like to see honest people duped by a designing knave & therefor I write as You see I have & hope You will use Your own discretion about the matter but I am confident that all can be proved if it was necessary but the law of Libel in this state is “the greater the truth the greater the Libel” You when asked about persons often replied that You knew nothing of them & thereby avoided the name of newsteller
Jewett is a man of first rate character & was from Midlebury Vermont & is proprietor of the largest & most repectable paper in this city even if it is a Whig paper he is a very good sort of a man withal & likes to see all things done decently & in order
Many men here believe he tells stories of his exploits that been falsity on their face & think all he tells of himself is equaly false as for his time here being worth 50 dollrs per day I do not believe that while here he averaged 50 cts per day & I heer he did not pay all the bills he ought to have done. I am sorry to hear that he could so easily dupe the citisens of my own native state but for all they are sometimes as green as the hills of their own state

title: neelsmith
text:
Transcription
Buffalo 1st Aug 1852
Brother
I find one of your letters dated 6th April & and I do not know whether it has been answered or not at any rate it has not been filed away & thinking perhaps you would like to hear from us here once more I thought to write to you a few lines
Of course in the first place we would write concerning our health which is at this time quite good at any rate is is passable – our wife has gone for a few days into the country on a visit to some friends & has taken our little girl with her she has been gone since tuesday morning & as I requested her to stay until she made a good visit I hope she will & probably will be home this week Our Boys are quite well & as it is now vacation they will be out of school for a few weeks & I wish they were with you that they might work & grow fat but you are too far off to think of such a thing at present
Our business has been quite good for this past spring since April but is now quite slack on & I am not sorry they hot weather makes me little inclined to work & as I have only a trifle to do it all comes round right
it is quite cool today however & has been since we had as fine a storm of Thunder & Lightning as one could wish to witness last Thursday night
Our brother Artemas is here & has been since last march to & perhaps may make up his mind to remove to this place to live at any a few days will determine he is quite well at present & has been since he came here he recieves letters quite often from Keeseville
Our Father wrote to me on the 23d & and I was glad to hear again from our Brother through him & also was glad that his garden was in so fine a condition & his health was so good he writes me that he has had a railing placed around the graves of these dear ones that are buried there where he no doubt soon epets to be laid by those that may survive him it is a melancholy yet a pleasant thing to thus make the place of burial of our friends our care & it gives us an assurance that when we too follow we may be held in kind remembrance by those left behind for we too must go
I know not how they manage there & who pays the expenses of the house but I do know that either of us would feel willing to contribute to the wants of our remaning parent & I hope you will find out & let me know how things are there that we may not wait until it is too late & when you do so write to me all the particulars
Our brother Hiram (whose wife was at your place the last I heard about her) it seems has not yet made his pile & has gone with W Thomas into another business a business that I am informed if done in any sort of order for & judgement is sure to make the partners rich that are in it if they are in the way of luck as the term is for an acquaintance of mine who has recently returned was in the same business only he was in the northern mines but was sick a great deal of the time & was robed of his cattle by White me who run them off but he says that it is a money making business I have seen a plenty from these places & some of them have been working near hiram & know him, I hope he may be returned to his family in health & rich
Buffalo is now close to Panton & only a short ride on the rail & perhaps you had better come & see fellow & his wife & children & city &c &c & the fall is about to come again when we shall expect some or all of you to see us here & if Cynthia is still at Panton I would again urge her if she feels able in body to come & stay a time with us by & bye when it gets a trifle cooler for some say it is sickly here but I think that possibly reports are exagerated there has been a few sudden deaths during the past week & some can be traced to the too free use of sour cherries & the Whig meeting at the falls
Perhaps I may as well fill this side as not so I will keep on until I stop – –
I would like to know from friend if he does realy mean to go to California or what he intends to do for perhaps I might get him a situation somewhere out here if he likes & you desire it & I hope you will write to me friend
Frances I wish you had come back with me when we were at your house last winter for I fear another so good time will not come soon & I know you would have here been pleased & when you wanted to go back I could easily have gone with you if no good chance offered to go with good company
I hope William & also my namesake will not forget that they have an uncle her in Bufa & perhaps the next time they come to troy with those sheep their father may give them leave to come & see us here only 12 hours ride you know & also that youngest one named after my dear departed mother I hope you will be spared to grow up & be like her for then if God spares me I shall love you even more than I now do
Finaly one & all write as often as you choose but & if I forget to answer write again & I will send you one of the longest letters you ever received
Peace be with you all
Your Brother
HG. White

title: neelsmith
text:
Transcription
Buffalo 2d January 1856
Dear Brother
I was glad to receive a letter from you once more & thank you for it
I am glad to hear so good a report of the health & prospects of your family & I was glad to hear that William has well enough to keep a school notwithstanding I do not like the calling much less to keep one in my native town yet it is better than nothing but if he is truly fitted for the place it is well, for in order to form others well one should first learn to form themselves a thing that I have not yet fully learned, but my reasons for not keeping school in my native village is because a Prophet is without honor in his native place I trust these remarks will give no offence to William
You talk of selling out & retiring from business What will you go at as you cannot be idle if you try as “Idleness begets Vice” and an “Idlemans brains is the Devls workshop” so you see you ought not to retire in order to take your ease & be idle for we read of one that said soul thou hast much goods laid up for many days therefore eat Drink &c Yet it proved a bad investment to him poor fellow if we believe the record and it is as true now as it ever was no doubt, but I was only joking You probably have some project in view and & know how to mange your own affairs no doubt
Hiram says I always preached to him in my letters while he was in California & probably you may think I am doing so now but it is natural for me & I cannot help myself but I will try
I know not whether you have any desire to see the west if you have not I advise you to create a dsire, for I assure you that eastern men have no ideas of its extent & growth until they see for themselves & until you see & know you cannot tell how much easier they can raise wool & everything else that sells, then you can, also if you have a desire to make money you will see it is the place to do it also if one desires to spread themselves there they will find plenty of room & if one desires large views of life &c there is the place to generate them, but you will probably get plenty of such from your firstborn who is there but joking aside you ought to go & see the west
I received a letter from sister Adaline a few days previous to the receipt of yours. by it I learn that she has been quick sick this fall poor thing she must have felt lonely enough in the old home almost entirely forgotten or neglected by those of her own kindred, but she says she was not neglected by the neighbours who were extremely kind to her
I see that you desire to dispose of the old place & say you will sell it to the first that offers be he Negro, Irish or French does it not seem to you to be a sort of desecration
I am right glad to learn that the affair at Burlington is so nearly setted I hope it is all satisfactory if not I cannot tell whose is the fault
I recd from Artemas a sort of schedule of what fell to my share & by it I see that you got the Bible I know not how the division was made & whether all was satisfatory & would like to know for it was written to me that some said that I should not have the Bible if others had to pay 100 dollars (more than I would give for all the Bibles (to use) in the States) I never desired it & thought that Adaline ought to have it but presum all is right & have never received a word from any one since the division on the subject only barely the schedule from Artemas, I wrote to him to keep all of my portion that would bring the cash & only send me the old chair spoon & Towels & keep the rest for himself until I sent for them, he is quite poor & I feel sorry for him & would like to do him good if I can but he seems to be bound for bad luck or to be kept poor & possibly there can be no help for him all I fear is that he may become discouraged & take to drink for relief & if I can prevent it I will try & do so, for you know that it is written that “he that seeth his brother needy & does not relieve him &c it is a hard thing to see a poor fellow working hard daily striving to stem the river & finding himself continualy going down for & at the end of the year farther down than at the beginning
I took the liberty to send you the “Age of Progress” a paper printed here & devoted to spiritualism as you will see if you read it, these lectures are all recieved through the raps by an uneducated girl one that has had no educational advantages but you will know all about that if you read & if you are pleased with the papers you can write me if your desire

title: neelsmith
text:
Transcription
Burlington Nov 11 1852
My Son Nelson
I rec’d yours sometime ago informing me of your welfare, Business & also requesting me to pay our Town Representative the Insurance Money on the Building &c I started the next morning to see Wm. Hickock, but he had started for Montpeliar I tried to catch him but could not the Cars went faster than I could at this time of life knowing he would be home on Saturday night I went early on Monday Morning to his House, but he had left, but I overhalled him at the Depo he said he had rec’d no line from you neither ware the Books in hands but ware with Weston I went twice to Weston’s office but could not see him I chanced to meet him He said young Smalley had the Books and not to trouble myself for he would call on me I knew Smalley called last year for the pay on Hiram’s Insurance People hear don’t send their money to Montpeelir when they want their Money thare is a Person appointed to collect it and when he calls I shall pay it I could not see you gave yourself and me so much trouble for nothing. I suppose in a Scaterd Population they do not do as in a place like this. I have no news only we had a New Moon a little past eleven this morning I suppose it will do you as much good as anybody I suppose your Tribe ?? has let you know prety much how the Election has gone I have no comments to make. Our Family are all as well as usual except Cynthia she is quite unwell more so than she has ben since Hiram has ben gone she has a continual cough She calls it a bad cold I hope it is nothin worse, she still thinks of going to California I do wish you would come up and talk with her and discourage her it won’t do to write because she would know I had writen you and She would be displeased I wish that you let any of your Family know that I have writen you on this subject for she would soon here of it I don’t say with an intention to do harme, you can tell the ?? what is propper in this case and let that Sufise She had a letter from Hiram las Mail he was well and doing as usual I do think it would better for Hiram to come back and take care of his affares don’t you but it wont do for me to say anythin in favor it what I have writen you is confidential on the Square if you please Hiram sais you have never writen to Him I read a letter from George a few days ago they ware well he says he has sent me two Blls Flour it has not arrived yet hope it will soon I am almost out I have a large hog and is fat it measuer five feet & 7 Inches round the boddy I inted to kill as soon as the weather is col. nothing more at present give love to all and come and see us Fens made or not made
Father
P.S. Adaline wishes me to ask you to let her have 20, 30, 40, or 50lb Butter. Butter is low here and hard to be had she will give you the highest Market price

Buffalo 2 Jany 1860 Monday eve
Brother Nelson & Family
Have you had time to think how strange it is to write or say 1860 — well it is a strange word & whether we may live to see its close remains to be seen
It is some little time since I have heard from you, then you were amidst the din & confusion of men – mechanics & artisans making & finishing your new house – not strange faces altogether but familiar for I know & You & Your wife know now that the country joiner manages to stay around until his face becomes as familiar as the old Housedog

Brother Nelson

title: neelsmith
text:
Synopsis
Ebenezer in Burlington writes to Horatio Nelson in Panton.
Although the immediate prompt to write is in reply to a “buisness letter” from Horatio Nelson, the family news includes report of Artemas setting out for California as a ’49er seeking gold. It is not clear how long he stayed in California. The census of 1850 shows Artemas back at home in Keeseville ten months later (September 19, 1850), but in letters of 1852, Ebenezer refers to him as being in California. ## Transcription
Burlington Nov 18 1849
I read your Buisness Letter and should have answered it before but have buisy in preparing for winter that I had no time I have ordered your paper to Vergennes which I suppose you have got before this you can have them on thursdays Hiram has got the money on your Note he says the Banks will not give a receipt for Monies deposited but he would send you the money when he got time. your Mother is prety well but I am rather off of the hooks at presant Adaline is so that She keeps about house She is not as well as Hirams Wife your Mother and I went to Keeseville a week ago last thursday to take our leave of Artemas who started for California a week ago las Saturday morning I saw him about two minutes on the wharfe at Burlington and gave him a final goodby he said he would write me from N. york but I have rece’d no letter Adaline wants you to bring 20 lb of Butter when you come to see us you undoubtedly will come in the Cars as that is the most genteel way of traveling now a days our love to all
Eben White H.N. White
this is all the pape I have

title: neelsmith
text:
refersto::Emma J. Hammond refersto::William Goheen Hammond
Hammond Letter 6
Date: Jan 10, 1863
From: Emmie J.H.[45]
To: “My dear Brother” (W.G.Hammond) [41]
Friday Jan 10, 1863
My dear Brother
I received your kind letter last Friday week were very glad to hear from you we thought that you had forgotten us. We were looking for you all the time. We thought that the Yankees had gotten you. We had the cake baked and had every thing ready for you. And thought Frank [1051] & you [41] would surely come, and we would have a fine time with you. Every person had it that you were married. You must come Home as soon as you get married. I want to see you very much. Lucy [43] went down to Aunt Peggy’s [?] four weeks age she said that she would come Home last Saturday but she did not come. Are looking fer her tomorrow. She was going sooner but we were looking fer you. Mayberry [42] was at Home he only stayed a week he went back to Liberty last week. he did not know whether he would get to come back or not. Lucy [43] did not get to see him. She has not seen Wesley [213] yet. Bro John [34] has bought another farm he bought Sam Phillips. he gave $5000 for it they are anxious to get out of the mountain-they will move in a short tine. Alice [  ] is staying here she likes to stay down here. She is very glad that they are a going to move she says that she will come down every day. black Nan has the diarrhea, she had it very badly but is getting better: The Dr. was there last evening. Well I will change my subject I want to see you very much I wish that you would come Home before long I would like to see Frank [1051] very much. Cousin Priscilla [ ] and Tabitha [ ] were here a week or two ago. They were down at their sister Elizabeth’s [ ] and spent the Christmas. I reckon you had a fine time at Christmas. I wish that you had been here then. Mildred [1808] was here and all of the children. She came down a Thursday and stayed until Friday, John [34] came a long and she went home with him. He bought a drove and took them to Staunton, he was gone three weeks. Mother [16] has her health better than she did when you were at Home, she has net been sick since you left, she didn’t like it that you didn’t come when you said that you were coming you must come home in the spring. We can’t do without seeing you any longer than then. Well I must close for I recken you are tired of my scribbling for this time any how.
Well good bye dear Will [41].
P.S. We are all well except the colds. Ann [ ] says that she wishes that you would get her a dress and send it to her.
From your dear
Emmie J H [45]

Hammond Letter 7
Date:  April 25, 1863 From:  Wes (Wesley Hammond) [213]
To:  Bill (William G.Hammond) [41]

Tinker Knob, Va.
 April 25th, 1863
Dear Bill:
As I have not written to you for a long time, I suppose you have been wondering what has become of me. I have been at home since the midst of last December - have written to you once or twice during the time, but have not received a line in return from you. I received license to preach at our first Quarterly Meeting held in January. I have preached three times since and have been traveling around with bro. Crenshaw on this Circuit several times. What I will do now I cannot tell. Crenshaw told me a short tine ago, that he wanted me as a Junior preacher on this Circuit. Whether the Quarterly Conference will receive another preacher I cannot tell. I will accept the appointment very willingly if offered to me, I will have to preach twice or three times a week, and that you know, will keep me busy as my stock of sermons is small, and no one to rely on  but myself for assistance. I want you to send me some pretty ample notes, send as many as you well can. They will help me and very much. I would like to go down to see you and my friends in Clarke, this summer, but I don’t think I can do so. I am rather afraid to venture down that close to the Yankees. Am afraid they might catch me and Coly. Bro. Crenshaw is very anxious for you to come up this summer so you can preach for him. If I remain on this circ. (i.e. circuit) I am in hopes the Yankees will run you off for awhile so you can come up and preach for me. I think I will like circuit riding pretty well. If I can only keep from falling in love with some of the pretty women Bill you know all about such things, from experience, so I need not say anything about such things to you. Didn’t you tell me that Frank [1051] said she was going to select me a sweetheart? I suppose I will have to wait for her. Tell Frank I am anxious to see her. Give her my best regards, etc. I cannot tell why it is that you have received no letters from home Some of us have been writing to you every few weeks ever since you were married. You may not get this so I think it hardly worthwhile to write much. A letter came here for you some time in the winter from your correspondent Mollie. I thought it was no use to send it to you then, I will send it with this if I can find it - if not the next time I write. It contained a present which I will not send to you - will keep it  till you come here. If you get this letter I want you to remember me to all my Clarke Friends and especially to Miss Sue. How are all at Mr. Strothers and bro. Frank Greene’s? Does Frank G. laugh at you any more about “poor Job”? I saw sister Crenshaw yesterday and told her what you wrote in Ginnie’s letter. She said she was going to write to her father and direct to Markham, If you know him and any letters come there for him have them forwarded. She requested me to tell you to do so, as her father does not live very close to Markham he might not get them if any comes, write soon am send those notes without fail.
Affectionately Yours,
Wes

Hammond Letter 4
Date: Sept 8, 1861
FROM: Wesley Hammond [213]
To: “Reverend Bill” (W. G. Hammond) [41]
____________________
Valley Mountain Camp, Virginia
 September the 8th 1861
Reverend Bill:
I have written a great many letters home and still more to friends but I seldom if ever get anything in return, being so often disappointed I have almost concluded to quit writing altogether. It looks a little like we will have to quit soon whether we want to or not for it is hard scraping to get paper to write a letter now. I have been looking for a line or two from you eccasionally but not one have I received. I wrote to P. J. Hammond [33] and Mildred [1808]and sent them by a wagoner yesterday. And to Eliza [39] a few days before to have me some clothes made and send to me. Probably she will not get it so I will state again what I wanted. One pr. grey Janes pants with a red stripe 3/4 of an inch wide up each seam, a fatigue shirt cut of the same kind ef goods. This is to be made so that it can be worn in or outside of my pants. You saw cur uniform and can tell how it ought to be made. 2 or 3 pairs ef socks, a pr. drawers, a flannel under shirt and a checked shirt with a collar made to it. Our clothes are furnished us but if we furnish them we get paid for them in a short time. Tell them if they have none of that kind of Janes try and swap for some other of the same color for the fatigue. I don’t care much about the color of the pants. I reckon I will have to ask you to get me the shirting cloth as I am about out of money and a strong pr. of peg shoes. No. 9. It is impossible to get any here or any where close. I wrote in my other letters that John Ribble was coming over here with a wagon and would bring them over. He is here now and as soon as he gets home he is coming back with a wagon and will bring them with the things he will bring for Smith’s boys [11], [28]. You seem to have it attended to. Sam [37] wrote to John [34] to have him a pr. of good boots he also wants 2 or 3 pr socks. *********are about all that I am obliged to have. But there are some other things that would be of some service to me if we takee up winter quarters over here. A pair mittens the red comfort I left at home. and a pr of shoes. Ribble is also going to bring Smith’s [11], [28] something in the way of eatables if they at home want to send a little something they can do so. If they do don’t send any cooked victuals unless they are sure they will keep. Smiths [11], [28] Sam [37] and I tent together as we did at Lynchburg. We live quite rough by here more so than if we were on the railroad. Others are getting boxes from home which made us wish for a little something too. A good cheese would be so good.. I wrote to Peter [33] that we were looking for a fight almost every hour. It has rather died away and there is not so much prospect for it now. I received the news a short time I wrote him that the enemy had fallen back. Our forces moved up in a mile and a half of them The Tenn. forces were about pitching into them but Lee would not let them. I have no time to write any news. Infact I deem it useless as I have Just written several letters hone. Sam [37] and I are well and standing up to camp life better than the most of the Reg. I would like to write you a long letter but I have not time. We are fixing to move ever the mountains tomorrow. I will leave this letter unsealed until morning and if I have time to write more will do. Give my love to Mother [16] and tell her I am getting along well. To Kittie [ ] and Bonnie [ ] and all the other girls. Tell Kittie I have written to almost all my friends but her. Will write to her if I have time and paper to write it on. Tell Ann [ ] if I have a good white shirt at home send it to me with the other things. Write me soon.
Yours sincerely,
Wesley Hammond

title: White family letters
text:
The American Antiquarian Society in Worcester (AAS) holds a collection of mid-nineteenth century letters to and from members of the family of Ebenezer White (1779-1853). The letters were apparently saved by Ebenezer’s son, Horatio Nelson White (1802-1886), and passed down through his descendants until they were donated to the AAS by Candace Smith, Horatio Nelson’s great-great-granddaughter.
The notes here document 38 letters. All were addressed to Horatio Nelson in Panton, Vermont, or to his son, Friend Adams White (1833-1895), while Friend was still a boy or young man living with his family. One letter is from Horatio Nelson’s brother, Artemas (transcribed here), and one from his brother, Hiram (transcribed here). Eleven are from Horatio Nelson’s father, Ebenezer White. The remaining 25 letters are from Horatio Nelson’s brother, Henry George White. The letters range in date from 1842 to 1860; after Ebenezer’s death in 1853, all the letters are from Henry George, living in distant Buffalo, NY, to Horatio Nelson.
The letters focus primarily on family matters: who is in good health, who is still on speaking terms with which siblings, how the garden or family business is doing, and above all else who is most delinquent in paying the debt of a letter with a reply. At the same time, they offer glimpses of both local and national events (a catastrophic bridge collapse, presidential elections, the California gold rush that drew both Artemas and Hiram to “go west”) and everyday life in the middle of the nineteenth century (colera epidemics, a state fair, the revolution in travel resulting from the new railroads).

title: Family history
text:
I’m starting by sharing transcriptions of the primary source material I’m collecting for family historical research. I’m transcribing and annotating these documents in an Obsidian vault. The transcriptions are directly exported to the transcriptions section of this web site. The annotations are used to build pages for individuals identified in the sources. You can browse the transcriptions
You can use the sitewide search (the magnifying glass icon in the upper right corner of each page) to find material anywhere on the site. You can explore the individuals from this index by last name.






TipFinding individuals



People who used more than one last name appear under each, so you should be able to find them using any of their last names.





I’m separately posting notes in the blog section of this site. It’s not my intention to develop any kind of overarching historical narrative. Instead, I’m choosing to write about isolated episodes and people I find interesting, and can document adequately to support my text. My intention is to post only about when I can link directly to the relevant source material.


I’m beginning (slowly) in 2025 by focusing on a collection of letters to and from members of the family of Ebenezer White (1779-1853).

see an introduction to the White family letters




In writing about particular topics, I am setting two limits: I won’t write about people with living children (as far as I know), or who have died recently, whether or not they have children. I’m struggling to define “recently”, but in any case, members of the nineteenth-century White family I am starting will fall within any boundaries I might choose.

Included in the 1850, 1860, 1870, and 1880 U.S. censuses were mortality schedules that asked questions regarding those who died in the twelve months prior to the enumeration. This database is an index to several of these schedules. The schedule lists the deceased name, sex, age, color, whether widowed or not, place of birth, month of death, occupation, and cause of death. In 1870 the parents’ birthplaces were added. Learn more…
