title: neelsmith
text:
Notes
Who is the author of this letter, William A. Jones, Druggist?
Hammond Letter 2
Date: May 2Oth, 1861
From: Wm. A. Jones, Druggist
To: Wm. G. Hammond [41]
____________________
Liberty, Bedford, Va
 May 20, 1861
My dear Friend
Your letter came to hand in due time, & I must confess I have been rather slew answering it, but you must think ef the bad example set me by yourself. Every thing is in a perfect stew in regard to the prospect ef WAR. Old Bedford has four companys in service & several tethers that will start in a few Days. I saw your Brother May Berry  [42] the day he started for camp he seems to be in fine spirits at the prospect of giving the Yankees a leaden Till mixed with gunpowder, he said he intended writing to you as soon as he arrived in camp, doubtless you have heard from him before this, when you write to him, say to him that I was truly sorry that business prevented my seeing more of him the morning he left (which was last Wednesday) he reminded me much of you in appearance & especially in conversation, I think he is full Brother of my old Friend W. Goheen Hammond, I have left the Farm & come to Liberty to take charge of a Drug Store for an old & valued friend of mind (Sandir Cobb) and let him go and fight for the right, honor, and                of old Virginia, I wanted to go with them but owing to my health they would not take me, so I have to stay here and help to take care ef the Women and children whilst the brave sons of Bedford are gone to get their rights, I believe if we would act more and (sic) talk less, and lay our cause before our blessed Maker with that faith that should characterize the true Christian, there would be no Civil War of Bloodshed. All of your friends are generally well and wish to see you, please excuse this short letter (as the mail is about to close) and write soon to your friend.
Wm. A. Jones
Direct to Liberty
Bedford, Va.

title: neelsmith
text: refersto::William Goheen Hammond refersto::Wesley Hammond refersto::Mayberry Hammond

title: neelsmith
text:
Notes
Hammond Letter 1
Date: December 2, 1856
From: W. G. Hammond [41]
To: Wesley Hammond [213]
(Original of this letter is in possession of dhs, a gift from Aunt Emma [26], daddy’s [8] sister, many years ago.  I have transcribed it here, trying to be careful to assure an accurate transcription. The original shows beautiful penmanship and other signs of a well-trained, studious writer. 
      DHS.  7 September 2001.) 
(Note:  Square brackets following a name indicate the person’s identification number in The Master Genealogist, the computer software program in which I keep family data. Example: Wesley Hammon [213], W.G.Hammon [41]        DHS 06 September 2001)
Emory & Henry College
Dec 2, 1856
Dear Wes [213],
After waiting long and anxiously to receive a letter from some of those to whom I have long since written your letter came to hand and was read with more than ordinary satisfaction.  I was happy to learn something it contained and others I was sorry to learn. Among the latter class was the information that Harvey Moore was teaching school in a place where it conflicts so much with Mr. Campbell’s interests.  I would not have thought Harvey, being under so many obligations to him, would act in such away toward his old friend and teacher, one whom he ought to revere as the guardian and tutor of his youth.  Such a course is a very ungrateful one. And one that I hope with not be pursued by many students who have been favored by such instructions as Mr. Campbell has so patiently given them in their younger days.  I now look back upon the hours spent in his care and wish that I had improved them better. If I had, now I’d be much farther advanced and the cost of an education would not have been so great.  Wes, do not put off till a later period in your course of Study things that you should now learned, such as the thorough knowledge of grammar and arithmetic, the reading of such books as will yield your mind a beneficial store of knowledge and fit it for the course of study you should pursue until you are past my present age.  As books worthy of attention I would recommend a careful and diligent perusal of all of Thomas Dick’s works. “The Wonders of the World”. - “Guide to Knowledge”. - “The History of the Commonwealth of Rome”. And a book title, “Harper’s Family Library or History of the World from the Creation to the Deluge.”
All of these books you will find at home.  The last one I read several years ago and am now studying Natural History which is nearly the same in substance as the contents of that book. So the study is greatly facilitated by having a previous knowledge of it.
So with most of the above numerated works.  You will find in them a great deal of what you would have to learn at College. Don’t neglect now to obtain a complete knowledge of English Grammar for upon it is based almost the entire fabric of a good education. Understand this art well and you will have at command a style of writing, without which the best literary men cannot hold a fair reputation: for it matters not how much “sense” a writer may display if he is guilty of grammatical errors he is not looked upon as an elegant or refined scholar.  Many students here pouring over Latin & Greek have but an imperfect acquaintance with this exceedingly useful branch. (that is, grammar)
Now, if I have not already wearied you with advice let me insist on you writing compositions too with all your reading, for the two together are calculated to improve faster than most any other course.  
I am still well pleased at Emory and continue to study as my only source of enjoyment, for there is nothing here like “woman’s smiles” to cause the thoughts to steal away from books.  It is now near the end of the present session and I must soon know whether I can stay here another term of 5 months. Since I am now situated I think it would be much better to remain till June as I now have my room furnished and am well started in learning and shall endeavor to improve the moment as they pass.  Tell mother [16] that I am faring well here and have excellent health.  I have not been sick since I came here.      I would delight much in seeing my old friends at this time, especially some of the girls; give my love to them all – to Mr. Campbell and family present my sincere regards. Tell them that I often think of them now. May prosperity attend them and all the associates of my early years.
Until I see you I hope you and Mayberry [42] will assiduously apply yourselves to study and improve much while it will cost you but little.  
I herewith send you one of my compositions. It is the first one I wrote after I came.  I will try to send you more occasionally as I get time to copy them.
Write frequently.  I am always glad to hear from any one – It was really funny about Harvey Moore loving Sue Medly so hard - I suppose she has cast so strong a spell upon his heart that he can’t resist the “magic power” and in the desperation of his condition will ______ her to ease his throbbing heart, now burdened so with “love.”
Remind Sam [37] that I wrote to him sometime ago and have not yet recd anything in return, and to Buck [40] I addressed a letter some weeks ago.  Tell Eliza [39] that I have been looking for a letter from her for some considerable length of time – I hope to hear from her soon.   As you are going to school now and can have plenty time write, let me hear from you often –Let me congratulate you since you hold the honorable position of Lieutenancy – My lessons now demand my attention.
Yours affectionately,
W. G. Hammon  (sic) [41]
(Note that the personal signature does not put the letter d on the surname.  Numerous early spellings of the name followed that pattern, and earlier still some spellings included two -a- letters:  Hamman.  Dhs 7 September 2001)

title: neelsmith
text:
refersto::Mayberry Hammond refersto::William Goheen Hammond refersto::Eliza A. Hammond refersto::Lucy W. Hammond
Hammond Letter 5
Date: Sept 17, 1861
From: Mayberry Hammond [42]
To: W. G. Hammond [41]

Fairfax C. H.
September 17, 1861
I have delayed writing to you for several weeks from the fact that we are almost incessantly moving, so often and in so many ways, that I have not time at present to detail all the movements we have made in the last few weeks, I will merely state that I have had the satisfaction of being within sight of Washington twice in the past few days, once at “Munsens’ Hill” and again at “Mason’s Hill” a few days later, from which place we returned day before yesterday. both hills are situated about six miles from Washington about the same from Alexandria, two and a half miles from Arlington heights, saw plenty of Yankees, was in good shooting distance of them while on picket hut was not allowed to fire. Our line of pickets is gradually closing in around Washington and Alexandria, but when a grand move will be made is hard to tell. We were all somewhat surprised the other morning on getting up to see large trains ef wagons leaded with ammunition, which evidently means something and what that something is, is easily imagined, The confederates have had several severe skirmishes near the chain bridge above Washington, which resulted, as usual in the defeat ef the Yankees.
Capt. Breckenridge’s Company arrived at our camp from Richmond while we were yet at Centerville, to take our place in the Regiment as we have been detached from the Reg. as artileries (sic). We will get our horses and cannon in a few days and then, you need not be surprised to hear of the O.D.R’s distinguishing themselves. Your horse, which you left with __________, (“May Berry”, I believe. dhs) died several weeks ago. whether bad treatment was the cause of its dying I am unable to say. But would not be surprised if it was not, The things you left in the care of Mr. Ford at Fairfax C.H. have not been disturbed by the Yankees, I left the book you gave me, “________ Rhetoric” - in his care as it was troublesome to carry. We were all paid off today, - $38.00 which was for only til the first July and for uniform. Since writing the above I have received a letter from Eliza [39] and Lucy[43]. Eliza said she would send me some clothes, which would be very acceptable, as clothes are very hard to get here. Even if the pocket is full of money. Tell her to make me a shirt dark calico- pair drawers, pair Janespants, and a cover or dress shirt made of dark colored cloth if it can be got if not it doesn’t make much difference Just so it will stand the rubs. Mrs. Jones of Bedford was kind enough to send me a couple pairs of socks. If Eliza [39] and Lucy [43]  can make me the clothes and send them to me by you I will send them by the first opportunity as much money as I would have to give for the same amount of clothes here. I will write to them soon. I am quite well at this time. Write as soon as this comes to hand, and when you expect to return.  
Yours in haste,
Direct to Fairfax C. H.     Mayberry Hammond.

title: neelsmith
text:
refersto::Theodore Buchanan Hammond refersto::William Goheen Hammond refersto::Mayberry Hammond
Hammond Letter 3
Date: July 30, 1861
From: T.B.H. (Theodore Buchanan Hammond)[40]
To: “Dear Brother” (W. G. Hammond) [41]
_____________________
Sentersville (sic) July 30,/61
Dear Brother [41]:
I [40] received your letter this morning. It found me in good health I was to see Mayberry[42] yesterday he was in the great Battle But was not heart. Now to tell you something about the fight at Blackburn Ford which came off on the 18th the day before our Brigade which consists of 3 Regiments under General Longstreet left Manassas and went down to the ford where we remained over night in the morning between 10 and 11 o’clock we drawed up in line of battle it was not long before the enemy came up in sight They came in such a way we could not see them until they was in 150 yds of us. They fired the first round. Then we opened on them. The fight lasted over 2 hours. Though the cannonading lasted nearly all day. Our less was 9 or 10 killed between 60 and 7O wounded which several of them have dide (sic) since. Our Major was the first that fell in our Regiment. The Yankees was about 9000 in number while we did net have more than 1500 ingaged There loss was between 8 and 9 hundred killed we could not tell how many were wounded as many was carried off as fast as they fell. The grandest thing that I ever saw was the fight between our Washington artillery and one of their Brag Batterys. That fight lasted over ___________ and 500 shots between the two batterys and only lost a few men while on the enemys loss was very heavy our battery cut down hole collums of their men. There men had to run off and leave that Battry several times, during the hole fight they had a battery firing on our hospital. The fire became so heavy we had to carry out our wounded, After the fight was ever they sent in a _______ of _________  to berry their dead in still of berry their dead they went to putting up a mast battery But they soon had to give that up we berryed some of their ded and the rest of them is still lying on the field. When night came on every thing was quiet and remained so until  the next night between nine and 11 o’clock when they commenced again nearly all Round us But they done no damage. After that turn they was quiet until Sunday morning between 6 and 7 o’clock when they commenced again. It was not long before it became a general thing for several miles distant The fight was heaviest at Stone Bridge they made a desperate attempt to brake our collumns at one time the Southern troops gave back some distance. on account of their having some fresh troops to bring in  there number was at least 4 to 1 The infernal scoundrals fought under our flag this _____ after the fight had become a general thing. By then fighting under our flag our less was much grater than it would of been at one time the infantry right up ________ for one hour and twenty min with out ever seacing  Besides the canonading which was kept up all the time. The fight lasted over ten hours, as near as I could come at it  our loss was between 4  and 5 hundred killed and 15 hundred wounded and the enemy’s side the less was over nine thousand killed and wounded  This is what there one paper states. We got over one thousand prisoners We berred some of there dead though there is a great many of them laying all over the country not yet  berryed. We gathered up there wounded though a great many of them dide before they could be tended to. We got at least twenty thousand stand of arms, and some 80 pieces ef artilery and 500 hundred wagons loded with provisions and clothing. Twelve of them was loded with shoes. 
 (Page 2. July 30/61 TBH)
A great many of them had there familys along to settle the country as they went. I found a great many letters they had writen and had not time to send nearly all of them wrote home to those friends to direct them to Manassus Gap. We found a sermon that one of there Preachers had written ____ to preach at Manassus.  That night his ____ (unit?) was incampt at Manassus. I came across one of there wounded  I asked him what he was doing hear he said he came to fight   I asked him what he eschewed to get for services he said he was promised 20 dollars a month and one hundred and 60 acres of land in Virginia. They have not got but very few of our men prisoners ____  few they get they have hung.  If that be true after this I won’t take any prisoners ______  ________we are camped  at Sentersville (i.e. Centerville) it is not ________ Fairfax C H near Sentersville ____________ .   After the enemy cannoned retreating Between five and 6 o’clock such running you never   heard tell of.  if we had 4 or 5 hours more to ______________.   General S____ was on the field  he made his brags that the Stars and stripes had never fell  But they came down on the 27th. Gen. Beauregard was on the field he rode up and down the line encouraging his men until his horse was shot from (under ?)him. Gen Johnson gathered the flag of a wavering Regiment and suceeded in puting the enemy to flight. Gen Davis was also on the Battlefield. A great many of _________ from ________  ________ killed and wounded.   Col. James Preston’s Regiment was there was only 16 of them carried out safe. A great many of them wounded. The Blacksburg company suffered considerably. Charles Runnalds (?) there.   his close was tore all over. But he did not get a wound several balls passed through his hat and a great many mark his coat. I must close I don’t knew how long we will remain here. I don’t think we will remain  here many days. I think we will move on nearer Alexandria.   ______direct a letter to Mannassas Gap I may get it. Our troops extend down in a few miles ef Alexandria I think the hardest Battle has been fought. We may have Battle that will last longer But they never will come so close to us again. This was there Brag army. They Brought in all the regulars that was in the United States …..  they had ten thousand Regulars all of them was in this fight. It is hard to tell how many troops they had. But it is generally thought that they had not less than eighty thousand. I must close for this time.
Respectfully yours,
T.B.H. [40]
P.S. Give  my respects to all inquiring friends.

title: neelsmith
text:
Henry George White in Buffalo writes to Horatio Nelson White and Syrena Adams White in Panton.
Horatio Nelson and Syrena have returned from visiting Buffalo. Henry George shares his worries about their brother Artemas, and discusses the arrangements ensuing on the recent death of their father, Ebenezer. (Note that Ebenezer was still alive and writing to Horatio Nelson in December of 1853, 1853-12-13-EW-to-HNW) Henry George also refers to his booming business, now up to 25 employees. ## Transcription
Buffalo 12th March 54
Brother Nelson & Wife
I have waited for some time to hear how you arrived home after your visit I recd a letter from Hiram who stated to me that you all got along well & arrived in Poultney the first day or night & staid 2 nights &c &c
We were both pleased that you all came out to see us but regret that it was so cold that we could not get around any better than we did as then we could have seen things better but as it is you will have to come again when it is not so cold, now you have learned the way it will not be as hard to do so
My wife was half sick while you were here with a severe pain in the side had too much grit to let me know of it lest is should distract from the pleasures of the visit, if it was not for that she would have gone round with you more, it was in fact caused by having to be with our girl so much but we do not always have such a girl mostly better yet often worse but the bad are off in quick time
I am sorry that Hiram found it necessay to leave the old home & his sister but so it is & I will note interfere I pity her, poor thing for after all she is our only sister I pity her
I rec’ed a letter from Brother Artemas he is in New York & was quite sick or rather he had been so, I hope he is better now, he poor fellow seems to have a long streak of bad luck or rather he seems to be going down stream. Jast I know how how it will be but I hope he will have a turn of luck soon if he does not he will become discouraged & perhaps drink for we know not how things will go with any of us so let us be kind to one another so that we shall not accuse ourselves of being accessing to to anything that may occur
My Business begins to start I now have about 25 men at work & if the weather holds warm shall soon be as busy as I desire to be
The weather has been quite warm all this month & the ice has left the creek but there is plenty in the lake yet to last for sometime to come I fear we shall catch it towards the close of the month for the old Sayings are sometimes true come in like a lamb go out like a lion, but in these days of spiritual manifestations one cannot tell what to think of
We shall always be pleased to have you come again both of you & will try to amuse you and also if Frances or any of the other children choose to come we shall be be happy to have them We would urge them if it was right to do so but as they have parents it is not
Yet if some one of your family does not come out here & see us I shall be sorry, I cannot tell whether the cholera will be here this season or not yet hope it will not if it comes will do our best to keep right & put our trust in providence & keep our barrels open as that is the best plan to keep it off
If some of the boys would write to George it might be the means of learning both to write & perhaps do them good if they write tell them to direct to my care as then he will get it
Hiram says Lenny wrote to him we hav not yet recieved it, I invite any or all of your boys & girls to write to us & promise to answer
We are all quite well at this present time but & hope you & yours are
I say to you again we were pleased that you came & hope you will come again we hav been to your house often & as the distance is short now let our visits be often
All unite with me in sending to you all the love & kind regards
Has there anything been done about a stone to put to the grave of “our Father” let us act in concert & then all will have a chance it ought to be done
The day has been beautiful & so is the night
Your Brother
H.G. White

title: neelsmith
text:
Transcription
Buffalo 1 April 55
My Brother
I have just wrote to Hiram & now write to you yet you both are my detters
Sometimes there is not so good a feeling existing as there should be between you all there & if it is so know perhaps you may not have heard the news about us here
We have another member of our family a fine Baby Boy three weeks old to day & that & its mother are doing quite well, better than I at one time expected for I thought that neither would survive but I feel thankful it is no worse
We here had a cold severe & bad winter & it is cold now & nothing for a great many to do & so misery is plenty among us everything is high & no work
I wrote to Hiram that I thought the best way to dispose of the BIble was to cast lots for it as that would be fairer than to put it up & let the one that had the most money to spen take it but cast lots for it & see who gets it. – or ask the spirit of its late owner who shall have it & she will make her own choice suppose you try that way – any way is fairer than the money way for it may be her wish for me to have it if so I would take it but if I was to bid against any of you her children my Brothers & Sister I would not give 10 cents I would rather imitate her example than have her Bible & if I had the Book without her spirit I would be constantly reproached. I have reproaches enough already
You ought to have taken these cattle of ?? & then allowed for them what they were worth to you & I would have stood by you in the matter & something would have been got out of the note
Settle up the concerns for the sake of peace & divide the old Jugs, Bottles, Corkscrews & other traps among you & save one old chair for me & I will be satisfied & for the sake of the money of our parents do let us try & live like Brothers “Love one another” if you love the money of her who raised us when young & helpless & if you desire to be a follower of Jesus do try & promote peace
I thank god that I live far away from all of you because I escape a part of the trouble & you do not hear what I am doing as much as you would if I were near you all, when I say you I mean all of you Nelson, Artemas, Adaline & Hiram
Live in peace & try not & love each other & remember that the spirit of our departed friends are constantly with you
Business I cannot tell how it will be this year but as usual I live in hopes
Money is hard to be got at & probably will be for some time I would like to hear from any of your children & wish they would write to me – I suppose it would do no good to ask one or any of them to come & see us here this season but if they write I could tell Friend, William Frances or all of you write to me
Give my love to all or any of my friends
Peace be with you & your family is my wish
Your Brother
H.G. White

title: neelsmith
text:
Transcription
Buffalo July 2d 1848
Brother Nelson &c
As it is a rainy afternoon and feeling little or no inclination to go to church I thought to write a few lines to You
As it is usual to begin by writing concerning Health I will say that we are tolerably well that is as well as usual which I suppose is first rate & we hope You and Yours are in a like situation
It has been quite sickly & is now so here diseases of a Bilious nature Billious Fever, Fever ague &c but we have all escaped as Yet, in the country as well as the city it has been the same but it appears to be rather abating now
Our Little ones grow somewhat although I would be glad if Charles grew faster, he does not appear sick Yet he does not grow & thrive as I would like, George is as well as most Boys are of his age & our little one the girl Ann Eliza (she of whom you wrote concening those shoes) grows finely & has every appearance of of being healthy Ann & myself prety tolerable well
Our weather has has been quite dry since April Yet we have fine coll Breezes from the Lake which make it comfortable
My Business has been quite good that is I have done considerable work but I do not know how the crop will gather perhaps it may rot in the Ground & perhaps it may prove a good Yield at any rate it is planted & I think for the most part in good soil I have had work for from 10 to 20 men since February
Having now given You a history of matters & things perhaps it may be well to broach another subject
We would be glad to hear from You & from all of our Nephews & Nieces & hope we may be fortified by the receipt of a Letter from each, I would send them a paper accasionaly but for that odious 3 cent prepayment of postage I wish all papers were free postage My Boy William I hope he will write another Letter & also Friend. Frances & George, Frances wrote a fine Letter which we have Yet & shall keep in hopes of getting another so if You desire to practice write again Frances
I have not heard from Home for some time & I fear we are all getting to be selfish & do not care to hear or write to our Friends now such should not be the case & shall not be on my part I assure You.
We expect you & Syrena out here this season & as the state fair is to be held here this Year in the early part of September we thought that perhaps it might add to the inducement for You to come for I assure You it will be a splendid thing & probably more people will be gathered here than ever before besides the Animals & other things usual on such accasions & You being Farmers ought to be interested I will write You again when it is to be if You desire & if You make up Your mind to come the thing is half done then I know it is hard times but money ought to be looked upon as a means given us to promote our own & others happiness We hope You will make up Your minds to come & also that will come for there will never probably be so much to induce You to come as now so prepare to come & start & You will be here before You thought of it
I usualy write over the whole sheet but now I think I shall not do so but You have my meaning without any palaver
I shall write to Artemas for I feel queer that any of my Brothers or any of my Friends should feel towards me anything but goodwill to be sure I told him some plain truths but as they were truths he ought to have received them as for his good, but I am not the only or first person that has made others angry by telling them the truth, however I have said all I shall unless I am invited to say more by himself, he is in a bad state of feeling towards his own friends & I hope it may soon give way to better feelings & I shall try & do what I can to promote the same
I think if You would just write to him a Friendly letter You would help the matter of reconciliation on in a great measure, for he feels as if all were against him & the fact of Your not going to see him or writing to him gives it a semblance of reality, so I hope You will write to him even if You have no especial Business
I believe that Hiram is the only one with whom he at present fellowships & they have been at swords points often
I saw or had read to me a portion of a Letter from Your neighbor Spaulding concerning a Doctor Allin that formerly lived here in Buffalo & my opinion of him was solicited. as it regards his skill as a medicine man I do not know much about it having never had any occasion to employ him or any of the paternity & I hope You will not. I have seen some that he prescribed for & they say that he done them much good but have but little faith in any medicine or Doctor & probably nature done as much for them as physic & therefor any opinion from me might be of little use to any one, as it regards that matter for which he was tried & aquitted here I think it to have originated in malice & falsehood & so did the Jury as they acquitted him of the charge
But one thing You will find him to be as all other John Bulls are a great Brag & as generaly they are great Liars also I presume he will not be an exception to the rule So you can gather from that my ideas
I am an advocate of cold water Temperance & they will in most cases promote Health & you can snap You snap Your fingers at the faculty & all Quacks & go on You may rejoicing
I have about Send to You the usual quantity of writing so shall as usual bid You good bye & may all the choice Blessings of Heaven ever attend You & Yours is the prayer ever of Your Brother Amen
H.G. White

Transcription
Sunday 2 oclock PM. Sep 9 1849
Nelson
I and your Mother went to church in the four noon, but not being much entertained we stay at home this afternoon, and I have undertaken to write three letters one to Hiram and one to A. & one to G — your Mother & myself are as well as usual Adaline has ben Sick 13 weeks She is better to day, but has ben worse Since you left us, Cynthia has ben down but (tear in paper) She Set up yesterday I have not heard from her to day, but shall see her by & by you Mother wants the Children to save a good bunch of Cale seed, for she has got some Birds to feed. I want you to save me Cloth enough for a pare of pantiloons for you know if I had 1400 sheep I would give you some & I should like enough for a Coat if you have it to spare. that I will pay you for, in somthing perhapes I will let you have a Mare or Somthing of that sort, we expect Friend, Wm & George to see us before Potato Diging I think Taters wont be so very scarce after all as they are selling for 25 ct per Bushel we have had no letter from George for a long time I wish I could learn the reason
Love to all
Father

Ebenezer White in Burlington writes to Horatio Nelson White in Panton.
Ebenezer informs Horatio Nelson about markets for hay and “stock,” and how the prices have been skewed by farmers foolishly trying to take profits by selling too much of their stock. He also writes about the difficulty in getting butter, as he does in four earlier letters from 1849-1852 (all dated between October 31 and late December of the year).
This is the latest letter in the collection written by Ebenezer.

title: neelsmith
text:
Transcription
Burlington Dec 13 1853
My Son
As it has jut began to snow I have began to write. I have nothing particular to write but I write to plague you knowing if you were not pleased to have me write you would write back I wrote you a short time since but have recd no answer neither do I expect any to this, and should not wish any if you & your Kid would come and make us a visit which I should — think you can as you can’t make Fence now I should be happy to see you or any of the Family we are all pretty well Cynthia has got about as well as usual we expect a letter from Hiram every night but you will git none from him untill you have answered some of his letters he thinks hard of you for not writing poor Fellow he don’t consider how much Fence you have had to make I wrote to you about Butter (it makes my han shake to to write the word) if you have any to Spare and don’t like to let it.have it let me have it and the Dimes are ready (as Hiram sais) I have not tasted of any Butter for five or six weeks excep last Thanksgiven there was a smal piece put on my Pudding and it got melted before I could git it off but we always have it upon the Table and shall if you come whether you bring any or not, but it will not be as good and nice as Syreana makes
turn over
the Farmers abot here have got themselves in a fix they have sold off all their stock they could that they might git four times as much for their Hay as it is worth the cold weather has held off so long that every body has hay to sell for they can’t buy stock to eat it up ho-ha-ha good I am glad Col. Smith and other good judges think Hay won’t be over $5 or $6 at the out side next march I mean per ton but I don’t care for I can’t eat Hay any more than I do Butter perhapes it may help you if you have not ben foolish enough to sell off your stock I believe you usually have more stock than hay I think we shall have a milde Winter although it is now snowing those Rains we have along back ware in the place of snows don’t you think so? if all the Rains we have had had ben Snow it wold be three feet deep if it had not melted
it is gitting dark so I cant plague you any more now but I will son if I am well good by
Love as usual your Father
E White
P S the California papers say thare are 16,000 people in that place

An exchange of family news. Ebenezer has recovered from the illness referred to in 1851-09-03-HGW-to-HNW, despite having taken “the Homipathice humbug.” Ebenezer is trying to stop delivery of a paper to Horatio Nelson and recounts the difficulties he has had getting the account settled up.

title: neelsmith
text:
Transcription
Burlington July 27 1851
My Son
I rec’ed yours of the 24 yesterday the day it was mailed I was very glad it had raind at your place for that I am indebted to you for a letter I hope it may rain often. I could not think of writing to you evry time it rains here for it rans almost evry day a more growing Season in the vilage was never known it Thunders now you say it is a long time since you rec’ed a letter from me I could say the same of you. I was glad to learn that your Wife & self have ben to Poultny and a happy visit that looks right. you and your Wif shold go among your friend & enjoy yourselves and not alwais be delving at home you have property enough, yes and to much if you had less you would have less on your minds I hope you visit George this fall I have a letter from him evry few days now the Potag is so cheap he says som-times he thinks he will never write to any of you again that you don’t care anything about him, if you did you would write to him I am glad you have had a letter from Hiram am glad to hear he is well we have not had a letter from him since the 20th of March which is over four months we think strange that he has not writen you know the Mailes goes safe now or ought to for there is an Agent goes with them the same as the British Mailes go though here I wish you would send -the- the letter to Boy Friend when he comes up if thare is nothing Confidential in it I hope you will not forgit it you may concider your paper Stopes on Tuesday the 8 of this month I hapened to take him ?? on the eving at the express office he said it should be stoped from that time perhapes he never will think of it again I advise you not to take them out of the Post Office if he should continue to Send them I told him we had caled a number of times to sittle, but no one knew how it stood he said he knows it, but he coud to make it out, I told to do so & it should be paid I requested Frances to tell you write about how long a time was Due and what the price was when you commenced taking it. for I saw Man settle with his foreman for one Dollar per year if I am not Much mistaken he acknoleged that Hiram had paid him money for you I hope Friend will be up and Candace for she has not been here for a long time we expect a great display of Firework better than that of the 4th I have ben quite unwell this sumr and was when the Children ware here. I was on the Bed when they went away and did not know where they went or I shoud have said. good by to them, but neither of them saw fit to say good by to their old sick Grandfather I felt Grieved at the time but I lay up no hard feelings towards them they are young. neither did you My Son think to enquire after your old Farthe in your letter but Thanks to God my health is much improved and am quite smart for so old a person I am almost as well as I was before I took the Homipathice humbug I don’t know of anything more to write but love to you all and may the blessing of God ever attend you is the prayer of your Fathe Ebenr White
PS. I had forgotten to tell that Adaline is well as usual but Cynthia has had ?? of Bleeding at the lungs as she thinks but is prety smart now
EW
H.N. White Esqr of Panton VT
I gues you cant read this what blunders

Artemas in Keeseville, NY, writes to Horatio Nelson in Panton, VT. Artemas dates the letter “9 month 31 day” but the post mark is Oct 31, 1842.
Artemas writes to arrange delivery of three kegs of nails to Horatio Nelson, and incidentally reports the death of an infant child in his family due to sickness, as well as eight victims in the collapse of a suspension bridge.

title: neelsmith
text:
Transcription
Burlington june 7 1852
My Son Nelson
It is with a bosom filled with Grief that I now address you I am grieved that I have a Son who –who– has a heart to neglect his natural earthly Parent as you done done it is over one third of year since you have written to me, neither have I heard from you either directly or indirectly except –by– by the way of Buffalo, and what is the cause is more than I can divine. I know of nothing I have said or done to merit such neglect and it grieves me to think of it, I am alone as it ware, and no one to cheer me or comfort me in my Old age, and to be neglected who has formerly held a friendly corispondane if nothing more, is as much or more than I feel able to bare, it wears upon my mind, I should have writen you before had it not ben that I was expecting something from you in sake of a letter but have waited in vain. I hold a friendly and kind corispondance with all your Brothers even the one who is seven thousands miles from me has writen to me since you have, living short of 30 what does it mean? thare has ben a corispondance caried on betwixt the two Families the contents of which I know nothing of as I read none of the Letter nor heave any part of them read. I hope it is nothing to make dificulty between you and me, but I have done with this subject I have not a heart or a wish to dwell upon a subject so adverse to my feelings. I supose you have had prety much such kind of weather as we have heare cold and dry I fear you have sufered more by the douth than we have on account of your land being more Claye, but should think that the land around your home premises would be apt to stand the drouth being much of it moist and springey, ledges &c which may in some measure protect you, but having lands scatered about as I suppose yours must be is very likely some of it must suffer I think of you, and am affeard that not only you , but many others must suffer, but the Lord knows what is best for us although we short sighted Mortals do not see it in the light our Heavenly Father does. My Garden looks as well as any of my neighbours and better than some I worked very hard, and beyond my strength this spring to to keep my Garden clear of Grass and weeds it neve was so clean before, both of weeds and vegetables although the latter look better than I could expect concidering the season I think I shall have new Potatoes in 4 weeks and those precious things Tomatoes that I have tried for five or six years to love and can’t beare the stinking things. I should think I have from fifty to sixty plants some of them ten inches high all looking very will ever so many Plants I stand ready to give to any one who may want. I wish I wish you had them –if you had them– if you have not a plenty, as I believe you & your folks love them I have set out my early cabbege and have plenty left which I shall sell or give to particular Friends. Fruit looks very promising Rasberies White, Black and Red never looked as well, my Cucumbers Squashes &c look will and well they may for it is so cold that no Bug or Flicor-lis to disturb them we have scarcely seen a House Fli this spring
I know of nothing more to write that you would like to of and perhapse you will care but little for what I have writen, but it will cost you nothing but the reading and that is no small job as many blunders as I have made you sai I do not write as well as I once did, but you are young and can write if you are a mind to, and I hope you will have a mind to. it is not likely you will have a chance to write me many letters and at the rate you have written in times past but very few I have all your letter you eve wrote me packed up that you may read if you please after I shall be no more —
I shall not mail this according to the date for I expect to see or hear from Hiram to night if I do I will write you give my love to your family. for I love you all. I pray our Hevenly Farther to put a right spirit within you, and bless you in spiritual and temporal blessings
Adieu
Your Father
PS. I do not ask any of you to visit me for if you want to see me for if you want to see me you will come without askin it is not likely I shall ever be able to visit you again but can’t tell what may happen
E.W
June 8 half past 4 PM.no Hiram nor letter or tidings we had a fine shower yesterday an other to day and is now sprinkling and looks likely for more for which we hope we all thankfull. Last Sabat night the wood pile on the South wharf belonging to the Steam Boat company was discoverd to be on fire which caused a great allarm, but was put out after distroying eigh or nine cords of wood had it hapened two or three ours later it must have distroyed perhapse the whole stores you know the wood lies close to to the west store the fire was discoverd a little before 10 oclock in the evening and last night it was set on Fire again about the same time of the night a Boat coming in gave the allarm and the two Follets being in the store they and perhapse others rushed out one on each side the store, and caut the Fellow, and on examingi him found Pouder and combustubles for setting fire they asked him what he did it for he said for Fun they put in jail he is a a lad abou eighteen or so, look lik a poor mierable chap I suppose they have had a court of inquiry to day but I have ben so unwell that I have not ben out today to learn further about it, I caght a terible cold yesterday Coughed a great deal last night and to day and feel as sore as if had ben to an old fashioned Raising. I am in hopes it will ware off, the lads name is Griffith & he does not belong to this Town
Adieu again Father

title: neelsmith
text:
Henry George White in Buffalo writes to his nephew Friend Adams White. Since Henry George is uncertain of Friend’s “wherabouts,” he addresses the envelope to Friend’s father, Horatio Nelson White, in Panton.
Friend, now about 19, is “passing the trying time” of his life, trying to decide on his future, which could include anything from farming, to mining for gold in California, to setting out to another location to find a profession or occupatoin. Henry George offers advice. He encourages his nephew to visit Buffalo, with details to consider about the deadly cholera that is seasonal in Buffalo.

title: neelsmith
text:
Transcription
Buffalo 19th December 1852
My Dear Nephew
I hardly know how to write to you or what about neither do I know where you are or what doing
I have tried so long & hard to get your Father & Mother out here on a visit that I have nearly given it up for a bad jobb & think I will commence with you in order to see if there is any of you that desire to see us but as I knew that you sometimes taught school & perhaps might be so engaged that you could not come I did not know how to proceed in the premises so I write to you at this time to find out your wherabouts and your plans & if you are not engaged I & are of a mind to come from & make us a visit we can fix it if your parents are willing so you can come & perhaps bring along Frances your sister
I do not know but that I shall come along that way if I come to Boston on business if I do I will write to you when
Although it may not be as well to come here in the winter as the summer yet perhaps your Parents might be better willing that you should come here in the cold weather as then there is no cholera or like diseases to fear but I hope that we have the same kind Father God or Providence to take care of us here that looks after your interests in Vermont & if he wishes to remove you he could find means to do so even if you were in Vermont or any where else, but let that pass for the present
We had some cholera here & many died & so many die when there is none, but there is something in that sound cholera that has a tendency to fill us with dread until after we get use to it – but there is none now & we hope to be excused for the next season
All your Cousins are well & unite in wishing you all a Merry Christmas & a Happy New Year Your Aunt has a very bad eye it has been so inflamed that she could not see her & was obliged to keep dark for several days but through the goodness of God & the use of Homoeopathy & Hydropathy she is better & is now getting along quite well & I hope will soon be well – I am as well as usual
It is now nearly one Year since I was at your Fathers House & saw you all in good health & spirits I hope you are so now & have been so throughout the season – but many that were at that time alive have been called home to report & receve their rewards
Say to your Father to & Mother that I have not forgotten them but always have hoped that they would come & see us & now that they can come as well in the winter as the summer in nice warm Cars & comfortable too I will accept of no excuse except a short crop & a lack of desire to do so for when they can come inside of two days they can have no excuse about time &c so start them if you dont come
Say to Frances that I suspect she does not desire to come & perhaps some young man resides there that keeps her from coming if so I ask it of her to make him promise to come to Buffalo & the Falls on their wedding tour at least she could not wish to refuse me that as she is too kindhearted
Say to William & George if they ever run away to come & see us as it is much better to be with friends than strangers in such cases but I hope they will not think of such things but be good boys to & so become good men & not bring sorrow to the hearts of their Parents
Say to Candace I hope as she bears the name of my Mother Your Grandmother I hope she will try & be like her so that all may love her & so that she can make all around her happy even as she did & then when she comes to be called home can go rejoicing
I do not know what to fill up this side of the sheet with but it must be filled I suppose so I will try
I know not what your intentions are whether to go to California to get rich, to go to some place seeking a place or occupation or to till the ground & raise sheep cows &c and be happy but what ever you do my young friend strive to do it well & fix your aim high & your efforts to correspond & you need never fear the consequences, only strive to fix upon something & keep it always in view & never forget your obligations to your Father your mother that bore you in her arms & to your god that cares for you & watches over you & to your self Ever keeping these things in view you may become an ornament to society and a source of happiness to your parents – you may think me preaching but I tell you that you are now passing the trying time of your life & you will look back & tremble when you think of it in after years for it is not a great while since I stood where you now stand & wonder at my escape & can only ascribe it to the good god who is ever neer & to the love I bore my Mother that I am here
Your Uncle H.G. White

title: neelsmith
text:
Henry George White in Buffalo writes to Horatio Nelson White in Panton.
Henry George writes upon returning to Buffalo from a visit to Panton with details of each leg of the long train journey home. He addresses each nephew or niece in order by age rank, and his advice to the children (now roughly ages 10-19) is a fascinating document of education and choice of profession in the mid-nineteenth century. ## Transcription
Buffalo Sunday evening 16 Feby 1852
Brother Nelson
I write to you at this time to let you know he arived safely here on Thursday morning after riding all night in the cars Log left Panton 7-o clock A.M. Wednesday made Vergennes 8 3/4- & left 9 1/2 made Rutland 11 1/2 & lay to 3 hours impatiently left at 2 1/2 & made Schenectady at 7 & at 7 1/4 left for Buffalo & arrived here at 9 1/2 having run slow & been detained somewhat during the night – so you see that after you are once underway you are soon somewhere I write this to encourage you to come some time & see us
I found our children well but our wife is & has been sick her side troubles her & while I was absent it sweled up quite a lump & is now sore to the touch but is some better I do not know what it will amount to & as I am so hopeful perhaps I do not realy know how bad it is
Syrena I think if you & Nelson both realy desired to come out here you could find a good time to do so but Your household cares have so grown upon You that You do not think You can leave home is it right to to be so tied to one continual round of duties & have no time for recreation & relaxation
Friend I was glad to see had grown to be so large & fine a looking young man but I noticed you were uneasy & unsettled as if you did not realy know what you were going to do next now I know how you feel & it is not so long since I was of your age but what I can remember all about it you are now of the right age to be laying plans for the future & it is right you are but it is also right to come to some conclusion & be sure you are right & then go ahead to & if you desire to go to College do so & if you wish a situation in some other business if you try you can get into one & if you desire to learn some mechanical trade or business do so but never learn the painters for it is a bad one & at the mercy of any vagabond who chooses to adopt it, be sure you are right
You talk of California now all the mining has been done heretofore in the river botoms & in such places that a single man could dig & wash his ounce or so as he choose in a day but those kind of times are gone by & hereafter the mining will have to be done by companies with a capital to crush the quartz rock & separate the gold & operations simply will not amount to much but probably as much or more gold will be dug as formerly you can make enquiries & read & you will come to the same conclusion – come & see me
Frances Ann was quite disapointed in your not coming back with me for I had promised to have you with me if I could before I left but while I was at Burlington I heard such would not be the case & I need not try so I did not we would be glad to have you come out here & stay as long as you like & as long as it will be for your benefit & Ann thinks she & yourself would both be pleased if such should be the case & when you will write us you will come I will find some way to get you here
William I thought you were a little sulky on the morning that we came away but I asked your Father & he says you sildom get so of which I was glad to hear you now have grown to be quite a large fellow & I hope your mind will keep pace with your body but will depend somewhat on your own exertion so I hope you will spend all or a large part of your leisure time in some useful study that will make you think & reflect & thereby give ?? to your mind by exercise for it matters not what business you eventualy follow knowledge will not hinder you So Read & think
George you were probably named after me & if so I hope you will try & sustain the reputation of the name I think much of that name they tell me you do not care for books &c I hope you will try do away with the truth of such an assertion
Candace I was glad to hear & see that you liked school so well & hope you will always be as apt & willing to learn I know you will read the book I gave to you & I hope you will under-stand what you read for there are good stories in that book as well as in the others & when I come again I will talk with you about them but I shall not come again until some of your folks comes out & makes us a visit & then they will probably bring you with them so ask them to come
Finaly you see I have written you all a slice not so much because I wished to instruct any of you as to say something & let you know how I thought
Read all the books & write to us when you have done so & let us know what you think of them all
I hope to recieve a letter from each of you soon. for I like to write & will answer
The bird is safely here & sings merrily & that with my bird & the children fills the house with music
Finaly may peace & plenty ever dwell where you dwell & all the blessings of heaven attend you always amen
H.G. White

title: neelsmith
text:
Hiram George White in Buffalo writes to Horatio Nelson White in Panton.
It seems to be a time of transition for all of the White family. Of Horatio Nelson’s children, his son, Friend, has gone west and writes fro Fondulac (Wisconsin), while William is sickly, which Henry George attributes to his school. The White siblings are still working through the settlement of their parents’ estate. Henry George’s business is prospering to the point that he has forty men working for him, but he would like to find some other, less demanding occupation. Hiram, previously engaged in the family grocery business in Burlington, is now a farmer, and wishes to travel west to see the country.

Transcription
Buffalo 19th Aug 1855
My Dear Brother
Your letter of the 31 July came duly to hand I was glad that you were all so well I rec’d one from Hiram about the same time which I answered & if you have seen him you possibly may have seen the letter I rec’ed a letter from Friend dated Fondulac at which place he still is as you no doubt know engaged in the Post Office
I hardly know what to write to you about but no doubt before I get through shall fill the paper
Ann had a letter from Mrs. Cock affair from her home which she styles clovernook she apears to be quite pleased & let us hope that they all will be ever
I have not recd any letter from Artemas since but no doubt shall soon My reasons for making him my agent was that as I could not conveniently be there myself & he could be it would save delay & bring about a more speedy settlement & regret that anything unpleasant should have occured or that any expence should have been made but however I hope all will be finaly setted to the satisfaction of all by the bye who has got the old family Bible as I do not onw whoever gets I hope will be able to realize that our Mothers spirit will still be about them while reading it & that if they are not made better by its perusal, they read in vain Verify may thoughts would be gendered by having & reading it
I have not had any letter from Adaline for sometime but no doubt shall by & bye when she gets ready
The weather usualy furnishes a topic for conversation & for Writing but no doubt you have the same kind there that we have which has been for the 5 days quite cold for August
My business has as usual kept me confined so I seldom get time be absent I have kept about 40 men at work which is more than usual for the time of the year & as a friend stoped with some days if he wrote to you of my perplexities & trails & of the effect upon me Moraly & physic-aly he will no doubt have given you to know my moral & spiritual state is quite low at times & so I desire to find some other business in which I should escape so many & constant perplexities which has a badd effect upon me – I do not expect to find any business without trials but I know that there are some which have not so many. but I find myself like a boy upon a sled going down hill who cannot stop until he gets to the bottom & so possibly I my continue in this until I get to the end of this state of existance – excuse me for the episod
We are all quite well & have been so our children all form finely & although they are not so large as yours it may be because they are not raised upon a farm & perhaps it is because that are not of so large stock at any rate they are not large nor as large as I could wish they were
I wrote to you to let William come out & see us during his vacation but as he did not come I presume he did not desire to do so – I fear his school may have a tendency to injure his health & so I wished to have him come & see us & possibly it might have been beneficial to him I hope he will not pursue his studies if they still continue to affect his health for recolect that you never plant & reap or gather at the same time & he may now be planting the seeds of some disease which may prove a trouble to him in future – but you as his parents ought to & probably do know if such is the case – but friend said he was sickly
I wrote to Hiram to know how it came about that he took a turn in his life moraly & what sort of a sect he has he said he had not as yet united with any but loved all & desired to follow Jesus to which I say god speed you & I would that all of followed him closely & tried to become like him – I hope he will even try & be like him as then he will become godlike & his state bothe here & after he leaves the body will be better for having tried to be like Jesus our example who came to lead us back to god from whom we had strayed
I do not know whether you ever believed that the spirits of our friends (angels) are constantly about us striving to influence us for our good but I do & the bible I think teaches the same & although I have not lately had any communications from my spirit friends owing to the presure of business yet I sill believe that they can & will communicate with us & that they still live & are sat far from us if we could realize it it would make us more circumspect in our acts & thoughts which are known to them as well
I need not tell you all or any any of you that we would be quite happy to have a visit from some of you this fall & as we have a baby which will keep us confined at Home you ought not to expect us there so send a delegation & let us known when you are coming
Hiram says he will go to the west this fall & see the country but as he is a farmer I do not see how he can until his crops are all in & then something else will be for him to do as farmers have but if I was in his place I would go & see the country & then I should know
I sent you a semon preached here at the opening of our unitarian convention I hope you read it in order to know how some of us feel you my think if I am a spiritualist I cannot be a unitarian I see nothing conflicting in them only find spiritualism to be unitarianist theories carried out & proved that is as man lives & leaves the body his state will be in future & that he can still if he desires progress toward god & a high state of spiritual existance
My sheet is full – Good bye H.G. White

title: neelsmith
text:
Transcription
Burlington Aug 9th 1849
Nelson
I thought perhapse you would like to hear from this region So I will write a few words to you and let you know how we are in the first place I am about the Same as when you ware at Burlington you Mother is pretty well much better than I would expect her to be considering the number of times She has had to go up & down Stares to attend to Adaline who has ben Sick ever Since you ware here about nine weeks in all She is confined to her Chamber & to her bed the most of the time Some days a little better and then back again no great alteration but if any She contineus to loos Strength but we are in hopes She will recover before long I have ben to Keeseville they ware all well and look prety slick about the premises Artemas has ben over twice Since you ware here he has ben in your neighbourhood twice looking for hay he told me he bough 60 Tons of Capt. Sherman for $7.00 per Ton perhapes he is now that way now giting it presed. I have had two Letters from George he writes that the Colera rages thare to an allarming degree but he don’t apear to be alllarmed he goes right amonst it if it becomes necessary I learned the same by a Man who came direct from Buffalo who took Tea with Geo. his Family ware well Geo writes to have me say to you that you had better take the Enquirer out of the office untill the time was out for which he subscribbed he thought the ware woth the postage and I think so to we call it now a good paper we all read it. he has since wrote me that he had Settle the subject with you and the publishers also think the must feel rather mean why don’t you write to him think hard that you don’t. Hiram & Family are prety well although his wife has had another time of bleeding but they are not allarmed we expected some of your young Folks up here before now but I suppose you ware affraid of Colra there has ben a few cases I believe of the real Colra but the cases have all ben traced to Intemperance or imprudance thares ben but two American who have died with it viz Mr. Stutson and Mr Lun a young man of 19 it is said by some that thares was not the real Colra the Widow Day Died a few days since with the Colra Morbus age 75 we are all dried up we shall have no potatoes I dont think I shall have half as many as I planted So you may prepare to find us in potatoes if we should live for you have had all the rain down your way we a good rain on Monday the Folks at the Grocery said it was on an account of Hiram’s going to Meeting the day before but I don’t believe it the Ground is moist down about Seven inches and I presum it is as dry as ashis four feet below if you are afraid to come up to see us yo could write can’t you?
our best Love to all tierd Father
H.N White Esq

title: neelsmith
text:
Transcription
Burlington Dec. 25 1851
My Son and all
I wish you mery Christmas we all ar well as usual except Adaline she has sliped down again and sprained her wrist so she cano’t use it I had a letter from George not long since he tells of coming out hear this winter hope he will had a letter from Artemas informing us of the Death of his little Hiram caused by canker Rash this is the fifth child he has ben called to part with by death the Lard has laid his hand heavy upon Him and often afflicted him in this way I hope he may have Grace to sustain him in those often afflictions. we have no word or letter from Hiram. you wrote of coming to see us I hope you will and bring your Wife & Candace with you and the Butter you told of and som Lard if you have it to spare for we have bouht no Hog nor do I expect to for thare is none to be sold. Oh! I want you to bring sausage enough for Me one meal – Cad Wainwright offers his place for sail which he gave $2200 and laid out $300 for improvements and will sell it for $1600 you know the peace it is short of a mile from the Court House not far from Willards thare is a Good Brick House and out Buildings. all in fine repair and two acres of land it is the place Syrereane thougt she would like to live on it is Dog Cheap the Buildings cost about twice the amount he asks for the whole it giting dark and I shall look for nex Tuesday noon my love to all
you Father
it said to be the coldest day we have had this winter best sleighin you never see we keep no Cow and have no Hog

Buffalo 27th Nov, 1859
My Old Brother
I have nothing especial to write but as I have just written a letter to my long brother at Washington, I thought to write you one, although you owe me two – this will make three – I excuse you because of the trouble & perplexities of building, finishing & getting into a new hous is something of a jobb as I know by experience – they call me a fool for building this house sometime s– hell I do not mind it much & sometimes they call me an old fool that I dont care for as I know of a great deal, but I do object to being called an old damned fool as that is rubbing it on to thick

District of Chittenden S.S.
The Hon. the Probate Court for the District of Chittenden.
To Noble Lovely Henry H. Mitchell and Mides A. Evarts, of Burlington,
Greeting.
Whereas application in writing hath been made to the Probate Court for the District of Chittenden by A. White one of the heirs to the estate of Ebenezer White late of Burlington in said District deceased, intestate for a division of said estate and the several persons interested in said estate have been notified thereof agreeably to law.
Therefore in pursuance of the statute in such case provided the said Court doth hereby appoint you a Committee and invest you with full power and authority for that purpose.
In discharging the duties of said appointment you will appraise all the estate of the said deceased now in the hands of the said Administrator you will then faithfully and impartially divide and make partition of said estate (after firstly paying the said Administrators the sum of nine dollars and eighty two cents ($9.82) ) being the balance due them on the settlement of their account)
page 25 in box
to and among Horatio N. White, Adaline White, Artemas White, George White and Hiram S. White, the heirs of the said Ebenezer White in the proportions following that is to say

To the said Horatio H. White an equal fifth portion thereof
To the said Adaline White an equal fifth portion thereof reckoning however as part and parcel of her said share the sum of sixty five dollars which hath heretofore been assigned to the said Adaline White in Pew No. 77 in the Congregational Church in Burlington by a decree of this Court she having accepted said assignment agreeable to law.
To the said Artemas White one equal fifth part thereof.
To the said George White one equal fifth part thereof.
To the said Hiram S.White one equal fifth part thereof.

When you proceed to the work you will give due notice to all parties concerned.

text: Bristol, Russel T., Panton, Vergennes p.o., was born in 1822. He was married in 1847 to Martha Jane Thompson, a daughter of James Thompson. She was born in 1828. They had a family of seven children born to them – Willard R. (married in 1876 to Mary A. Richards, or Cornwall, Vt.), Edwin S., Ernest J. (married in 1878 to S. Imogene Harris), Carlton D. (married in 18767 to Anna M. Elitharp, of Bridport, Vt.)), Alice J. (married in 1881 to Sidney M. Harris), Arthur H., and Wallis H. (married in 1886 to Cornelia L. Sibley). Russel T. Bristol was a son of Noah anna (Stafford) Bristol. Anna was born in Essex, Essex county, N.Y. in 1794, and died in Panton, Vt., in 1865. Noah was born in Panton, Vt., in 1789, and died in 1838. They had a family of nine children born to them. Three sons and one daughter are now living – Philemon L., Russel T., Abel,, and Mrs. Abigail Eno (now the wife of Rufus Eno). Those deceased are Philo (who died in 1885, aged seventy years), Stafford (who died in 1848, aged twenty-two years), Sybil (who married Watson Morgan and died in 1868, leaving a family of four children), Lydia (who married Charles Hayward and died in 1876, leaving a family of three sons). Noah Bristol was a son of Aaron and Sybil Bristol, who were natives of Harwinton, Litchfield county, Conn., and settled in Panton, Vt. 1785. Aaron Bristol was born in 1742, and died in 1823. They had a family of eight children – Sybil, Chauncey, Levi, Rhoda, Lemon, Olive, Moses and Noah. Moses and Noah inherited the homestead by will from Aaron, and remained as partners until the death of Moses in 1826. He was born in 1786, and served in the War of 1812.

In the name of god Amen, I Philip Euliss of orange county state of N Carolina being of sound and perfect mind and memory (blessed by god) do this nineteenth Day of July in the year of our Lord one thousand Eight hundred and twelve make and publish this my last will and testament in manner following that is to say, first I give and bequeath to my beloved wife Elizabeth one cow one bed & bedstead and furniture fitted out to her notion one Iron pot one skillet one Dish one spinning wheel three plates six spoons one chest one Bason all of her chairs also all her wearing clothes, secondly it is my will that my land be Divided into three Equal parts and sold separately at publick sale with all the rest of my property the money arising therefrom to be Distributed, as follows that is to say, to my beloved wife Elizabeth one twelfth part, the Balance to be divided among my Children as follows, my sons Henry Euliss, John Euliss and Adam Euliss and daughters Margaret Wimbro, Mary Linn, Molly Huffman, Eve Ross and Susanna Wimbro, to have Equally alike, my daughter Elizabeth Jones to have fourteen dollars Less than the above Equal shares, my daugther Barbara Tracy to have six Dollars Less than the above Equal shares, it is my will that the Children of my Daughter Catharine Lineberry have a share Equal to the above Equal shares that is to say her daughter Elinor Jones, to have one half of said share, her other children namely Sophia Coble George Lineberry and William Lineberry to have the other half Equally Divided among them –
and I hereby make and ordain my two sons Henry Euliss and John Euliss Executors of this my last will and testament In witness whereof I the said Philip Euliss have to this my last will and testament set my hand and seal the day and year above written
Philip x Euliss
his mark
signed sealed published and declared by the said Philip Euliss the testator as his last will and testament in the presence of us who were present at the time of signing and sealing thereof –
James Thoms Hadley

In the name of God Amen. I, Marmaduke Vickory, Sen., of the County of Randolph and the State of North Carolina, Planter, Being Sick and Weak in body but of perfect mind and memory, Thanks be given to God for the Same, Calling to mind the mortality of my Body and knowing that it is appointed for all men once to die, do make, ordain and appoint this my Last Will and Testament in manner and form as follows. First of all, I Recommend my Soul to God that gave it and my body to the earth to be Buried in Christian Burial at the Directions of my herin after named Executor and as touching my worldly Estate which God hath pleased to bless me with in this Life I give, devise and dispose of the same in the following manner and form. Item. I give unto my well beloved wife Elizabeth Vickory the full possession of my Dwelling house with all of my household goods and furniture during her Natural Life and at her decease to be disposed of in manner and form as follows———Item. I give and bequeath to my Beloved Son Samson Vickory all my lands and Tenements Except that part conveyed to my Grandson Marmaduke Vickory Second by Deed of gifts bearing Date December the Twenty fifth day one thousand Seven hundred and Eighty Seven— Item I give and bequeath to my son Samson Vickory all my personal Estate of Every kind quality and Specie to be possessed by him and possession of my Dwelling house with all the household furniture freely to be possessed by him with all the Benefits thereunto belonging and I do appoint the Son Samson Vickory and him alone to be my Executor of this my Last Will and Testament In Witness Whereof I have set my hand and seal this twenty Seventh day of December and in the year of our Lord on thousand seven hundred and Eight seven.

In the name of God Amen.
I Duncan Neil of the County of Coffee and State of Tennesse being weak in body but of sound and perfect mind and memory, considering the uncertainty of this ?morta? and being of sound ? Blssed be almighty God for the same do make and publish this my last will and testament in ?? and form following that is to say
Item 1st I give and bequeath my soul unto God who gave it.
Item 2nd I give and bequeath unto my beloved wife Betty the issue of one hundred and fifty dollars with her bed and bedding.
Item 3rd I do also give and bequeath unto my some James Neil the plantation where I now live on with all my lands on the south side of the Duck River running to John Carrolls spring Branch
I also will and bequeath to my beloved wife Betsy her life estate on the land while she remains a widow or see cause to stay on the land tho ?? in that case the profets arising from the land ceases be hers and the profits arising from the land to go to my two yougest James Neil and Angelina Neil and they are to be educated on the profits arising therefrom
I also will and bequeat unto Elizabeth Neil her life estate on the land where I now? live with wood and water – and land for any cultivate she sees proper so long as she rmains single and sees proper to live on the land there and in that case her claim or Claims to cease on said land.
And al lmy moveable property to be sold and the proceeds divided among the following heirs excepting my servant John who shall not be sold under six years after my decease but shall remain as a slave on the plantationa for the benefit of the family who resides there and then to be sold and to be desposed of as the balance of the property. –
I do also make Elizabeth Neil my lawful heir to her part of the property – this is to be sold, ?LeKeroisa? Thomas Neil Ellen Campoeso Alexander Neil Mary Oldfield Susan Hardaway Rachael Yell Angelina Neil al my lawful heirs as for William Neil and James Neil they have received their part excepting five dollars each
I appoint my sone Alexander Neil administrator of this my last will and testament hereby resolving all former wills by me made
In witness copies of I have hereunto set my hand and seal the 20th day of November 1840.
Duncan Neil
Signed sealed and published here by the above named Duncan Neil to be his last will and testament in the presence of us who have hereunto subscribed our names as witnesses in the presenc of the testator
Daniel Hardaway John Penn attests

H. G. WHITE DEAD.

Buffalo’s Oldest Citizen Died Suddenly at His Home on Irving Place.

In the death of Henry George White, Buffalo loses its oldest resident as well as an estimable citizen. He was born in Burlington, Vt., June 8, 1814, and died at his home, 32 Irving Place, at 6 o’clock this morning. Death, although resulting from old age, was unexpected. Last night Mr. White retired as well as he has ever been during the past two years, and this morning he was discovered dying by one of the members of the family. A physician was summoned, but the dying man expired as the physician crossed the threshold.
Mr. White, who would soon reach his 90th year, came to this city in 1836, full of the energy and ambition of youth. He had great faith in Buffalo’s future. Immediately on his arrival he started to learn the painter’s trade in all its branches. So well did he succeed that in 1838 he bought out the business and good-will of his employer, and thus, while just beginning his 25th year, he became his own “boss” and remained one ever since. His place of business was at 53 Main street, where he remained for over half a century.
Some years ago he formed a partnership with William H. Pinck and the business was then carried on under the name of White & Pinck and still continues under that name. For several years previous to the time of his death Mr. White refrained from participating in the active business of the firm, although still retaining his interest in the establishment.
He was married three times. In 1840 he married Ann Quayle of the Isle of Man, Eng., who died in 1860. Four children were born to them, and the following three are now living: George W. White and Charles H. White of this city and James H. White of Anadarko, Oklahoma. In 1862 he married Susan N. Prince, belonging to the well-known Prince family of this city, who died in 1864. In 1865 he married Susan D. Church of this city, who survives him. One son was born to them, Eugene R. White, editor of the Niagara Falls Gazette, and formerly a member of the editorial staff of the EVENING NEWS.
As to polltical bellef Mr. White was a Republican, although the first President for whom he cast a vote was the fiery Andrew Jackson. He was closely connected with the work of the Church of Our Father, of which he was one of the founders, and although a strict Unitarian by faith, was always willing to allow for the religious belles of others.
The funeral will take place from the family residence at 3 o’clock tomorrow afternoon.The Rev. Frederick Brown, pastor of the Church of Our Father, will officiate.

Aged Lady Dead.
Funeral of Mrs. Rush at Famer Monday – Well Attended.
The funeral of Mrs. Sallie Rush was conducted at Farmer Monday morning at 11 0’clock, and was attended by a large number of relatives and friends from Asheboro. Rev. B.F. Fincher conducted the service.
Mrs. Rush was 86 years old and was a highly respected lady. She had been in declining health for several months and her death Sunday was due to old age.
The deceased was the mother of our townsmen, Z.F. and Harris Rush and Mrs. Nereus Lowe, of Mechanic. Her husband was the late Noah Rush.
The bereaved relatives have the sympathy of a host of friends in the county.

C. H. Rush (Special to Daily News)
Asheboro, Dec. 16. – C.H. Ruish, 83, formerly superintendent of the water and lights department of Asheboro, died at his home on Academy street tonight at 7:30 o’clock after a prolonged illness. H was for many years railway express agent on the Asheboro and Aberdeen railroad.
Surviving are five children, C. Rush, chief of the Asheboro fire department; Mrs. Agnes Barker and Mrs. T.E. Lassiter, both of Asheboro; Mrs. Mona Rush Smith, Cambria, Va., and Mrs. J.P. Meador, of Aberdeen. Also surviving ar a sister, Mrs. Mary Jane Lowe, Asheboro, seven grandchildren and one great-grandchild.
Funeral service will be conducted at the First Methodist church at 11 o’clock Friday morning by the pastro, Rev. H. P. Powell. Interment will follow in the Asheboro cemetery. Mr. Rush was a lifelong member of the Methodist church.

Rutherford Farmer Is Buried Today

Mr. J.G. Greene Moved Here From Bedford County Fifteen Years Ago

Mr. J.G. Green the venerable father of Mrs. I.N. Gattis, died Monday afternoon at 3 o’clock at his home on the Shelbyville road about 2½ miles south of Murfreesboro, aged 84 year, 9 months and four days.
Mr. Green was a Union soldier and a pensioner. He was a member of the Methodist Church and a man of fine character and was highly esteemed.
Mr. Green came to this county from Bedford about fifteen years ago, and has since resided on his farm purchased at that time. He is survived by his wife and two children, Mrs. Gattis and Joe Green of Nashville. Funeral services were conducted this afternoon at 2:30 o’clock at the home of Mrs. Gattis on South Church street by Dr. John Baggett, Interment at Evergreen Cemetery.

title: Introducing the White letters project
text:
I’m beginning the blog section of this personal website with a project that promises to keep me busy for a while. The focus is a collection of unpublished letters now in the American Antiquarian Society in Worcester (AAS) to and from members of the family of Ebenezer White (1779-1853) in the mid-nineteenth century.1 The letter writers include farmers, grocers, a former ferry pilot, and failed forty-niners. Although Ebenezer’s eldest son Horatio Nelson White achieved some local prominence as a civic leader in the town of Panton and his younger brother Henry George White earned recognition for his work in the stained glass industry in Buffalo, New York, the Whites were not famous or always prosperous: much of the correspondence in fact centers on Ebenezer’s constant challenges trying to scratch out a living in Vermont, and of his sons’ attempts to find a better life somewhere else.
These very ordinary people are documented in a treasure of sources I could only fantasize about when I was working professionally as a scholar of the ancient Mediterranean world. The Vermont Historical Society in Burlington holds a collection of the business papers of Ebenezer and his son Hiram. The complete inventory of Ebenezer’s possesions when he died intestate was an accounting nightmare (and a source of tension in letters among Ebenezer’s sons), but the archival records of the court proceedings offer us a rich trove of material. Nineteenth-century newspapers fill in and confirm details of their lives. To those existing sources, I’m contributing transcriptions of the letters, and will post notes about them here as I work through the sources.
For starters, I’ve put together a brief overview with a checklist of the letters. Links in those notes lead to automatically assembled pages pulling together other documentary sources I have transcribed and indexed to individuals appearing in the White letters. If the clusters of documents sometime seem haphazard, I hope they will make more sense as the body of transcribed material grows.

title: Neel Smith: personal site
text:
On this site I’m sharing some of my research on topics not connected to my professional work. In one way or another, most of it concerns the history of my children’s family. Currently, the site includes a little background context, and a blog section where I’m sporadically posting notes.
I’m interested more generally in how to do historical research and use historical sources in writing for digital platforms. Future posts may also include some “DIY” notes on how I’m carrying out different parts of my research.



All pages on this web site have a “published” data showing when the published page was last updated. In the “Posts” section, notes are sorted by date, so if you peek there, you’ll see newest additions on top.
There’s also an  RSS feed if you prefer to automate notification of updates.






TipMy professional work on line



I have a separate web site where I’m posting some of my current on-line professional work, currently focused primarily on using language models to understand the syntax of historical languages like Greek, Latin and Hebrew. You can find it at https://neelsmith.github.io/.
